sources.news_title: Flock announces privacy updates to its car-tracking cameras | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Flock announces privacy updates to its car-tracking cameras
Flock Safety, a company facing increasing scrutiny of its nationwide car-tracking technology, announced several updates today that it said would improve privacy protections and prevent misuse.
The company’s network of 120,000 cameras, which can read license plates, are used by 7,000 law enforcement agencies across the country. Police departments say the systems help solve crimes. But reports of misuse by law enforcement, along with anxiety over the technology’s ability to surveil ordinary people, has led to protests and prompted some cities to end their contracts with the company.
“I realized we had a responsibility to do more,” said Garrett Langley, CEO of Atlanta-based Flock.
Some cities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, have stopped using Flock cameras in order to prevent immigration authorities from accessing their data. To provide more local control, the company said today that it would allow individual police departments to restrict what other law enforcement agencies can see — allowing them, for example, to access data to find stolen vehicles but not for immigration violations, the company said. It also is shortening the default time for data retention to a week, down from 30 days, though departments could change those settings.
Reducing the length of time data is retained is a positive development, said Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel from the American Civil Liberties Union. But he noted that it is easy for police departments to keep the data for longer.
The heightened local control, too, is “good in theory,” Marlow said, but has never been proved to work. A similar program was rolled out last year to block impermissible searches, he said, but Flock customers quickly found a workaround.

“When you put all this together, what you see is Flock treating privacy issues as public relations issues,” he said. “Flock is giving this response because it knows its company is in serious, serious trouble.”
Langley said the updates have been in the works for months. Although Flock announced steps to assuage privacy concerns, critics still view legislative changes as the ultimate avenue to rein in surveillance tech like Flock’s.
“What we need are laws,” said Barry Friedman, law professor and faculty director of the Policing Project at New York University. “The government should never be collecting our information without a law that gives it authority.”

sources.news_title: Flock Announces Platform Changes After Public Backlash to Its Camera Network
sources.text:
Surveillance technology giant Flock Safety announced sweeping changes to its platform on Aug. 13 aimed at addressing concerns over data access, privacy, and cases of law enforcement members allegedly abusing its camera network.
Flock, one of the largest providers of automated license plate readers (ALPRs) in the nation, operates a growing network of cameras that feed vehicle characteristics and plate data into its platform, which can be accessed by thousands of law enforcement agencies.
The company has faced increasing scrutiny in recent months by citizens, lawmakers, and civil liberties advocates following concerns over data retention and reports of misuse, as well as incidents of innocent motorists being mistakenly pulled over after an ALPR made a false match on their vehicle.
Flock stated that it is changing the retention time for its ALPR data from 30 days to a week, as well as rolling out “evidence mode” for law enforcement.
“Our analysis shows that over 90% of searches without a full plate are done within a week,” the company said in a statement. “Evidence Mode, which will roll out in the coming weeks, addresses the exceptional cases that take longer: detectives can preserve specific ALPR data as evidence for an active investigation in cold storage, consistent with existing laws and policies.”
Flock founder and CEO Garrett Langley said in a video statement that this means that “every image our cameras capture is by default purged from the customer’s database after one week, unless it becomes evidence in an active criminal investigation.”
Abuse of its technology, “at any level, is unacceptable,” Flock said. The company will begin requiring all law enforcement agencies using its cameras to adopt its “audit assistance” technology by the end of the year.
The feature is designed to detect abnormal activity on the company’s platforms and flag it for administrator review.
“In recent weeks, those reviews have been associated with arrests of several law enforcement officers who allegedly abused the system,” Flock said.
The officer’s arrest was the latest in a series of related incidents of law enforcement officers accused of accessing Flock camera data for non-work-related reasons, with dozens of cases linked to officers allegedly stalking romantic interests.
In addition to audit assistance, Flock said on Aug. 13 that it will also institute a policy called “proactive lockout,” which will automatically suspend access to its databases whenever a user’s activity is flagged as abnormal behavior.
In response to reports of mistaken arrests and traffic stops after Flock cameras mistook the cars of innocent motorists for target vehicles, Flock stated that “an alert is a lead, not a conclusion, which should be confirmed by an officer.”
“Before an alert goes out, the Flock system matches both the plate and the issuing state against the hotlist record. The system then filters out low-confidence reads before sending alerts to officers,” Flock stated.
“The final safeguard is human. Before acting, an officer visually confirms the plate and confirms the stop complies with law and agency policy. No stop should ever rest on an unverified alert standing alone.”
Langley confirmed that an unverified ALPR alert alone is not enough lawful basis for a traffic stop.
“Officers should verify that the vehicle matches the alert, that the alert is still active, prior to taking any type of enforcement action,” he said.
In an Aug. 13 blog post, the American Civil Liberties Union stated that Flock shortening its evidence retention window “may be a step in the right direction.”
However, the organization described Flock’s other changes as “retreads of previous inadequate safety measures.”

sources.news_title: Flock's answer to its surveillance scandals: trust us
sources.text:
On Thursday, the surveillance technology company Flock announced that it will limit access to its network of over 120,000 automatic license plate readers following disturbing reports dating back to at least 2021 of police officers abusing the technology for criminal activities like stalking.
In his blog announcement, Flock CEO Garrett Langley did not mention the widespread public backlash against the technology, which, in significant part, led more than 20 local governments to begin rolling back their use in July. He only stated that the policy updates work to address “three areas that are critical to the company: strengthening privacy, accountability, and security.”
Among the updates: Flock is now making mandatory a previously optional feature that flags “abnormal activity” for review, shortening the default recommended data storage period for Flock surveillance products from 30 to seven days, and establishing optional limits on data sharing between police departments.
The ACLU said in a Thursday statement that most of Flock’s policy changes are “merely retreads of previous inadequate safety measures” it highlighted last month. While Flock claims its new policies will empower local police to dictate what other users can and cannot search their data for, the nonprofit said the company is assuming that its system already prevents improper search queries.
Clearly, this isn’t the case. In a statement, Tom Bowman, the policy counsel for security and surveillance at the Center for Democracy & Technology, said that the policy changes are still “asking thousands of police departments to police themselves, despite evidence from across the U.S. that this lack of guardrails is unsafe.”
In other words, Flock’s answer to a crisis of trust is to ask for more of it.

Flock CEO unveils new privacy policy: 'We're not Big Brother'
sources.text:
Flock backpedals as nation revolts against surveillance devices
Controversial surveillance technology company Flock Safety has unveiled sweeping new privacy "guardrails," seemingly intended to quell growing unrest over its devices' presence across the country.
Days prior, CEO Garrett Langley went on a media run to convince the public that the company was not the latest cog in a dystopian surveillance state, but rather a purveyor of public safety. "We’re not Big Brother," said CEO Garrett Langley. "We’re focused on protecting people."
But many still wonder, if it looks like Big Brother, and it talks like Big Brother...
You May Also Like
What is Flock's new privacy policy?
Under the new policy, Flock will be adjusting its default data retention period from a 30 days to seven. Prior to this, Flock systems were automatically set to store an individual's registration and location information for a full month, but this can still be changed to longer or shorter periods according to state and local policy. The ACLU has previously recommended that data retention defaults be set to 48 hours.
In addition, Flock will now require law enforcement agencies to use a case code that delineates a potential offense before searching the Flock database. Previously, this was an optional setting for Flock clients, and dozens of law enforcement officers have been accused of using the database to stalk and harass individuals. The company's "Audit Assistance" tool, intended to flag inappropriate uses, will become standard on all Flock packages.
Flock is also adding a new feature called "Offense filtering for sharing." The tool will let cities moderate how other agencies access their residents' data by categorizing which types of offenses are searchable.
Does this make Flock cameras safer?
All of these changes come with exceptions. "Every community will continue to choose the retention period that fits its public safety strategy," according to Flock.
The company also announced a new "Evidence Mode," which allows law enforcement to bypass retention policies and store specific ALPR data if it is deemed evidence in an active investigation. The feature could be a step in the right direction, or it could make everything worse, according to civil rights groups.
"If 'Evidence Mode' only retains hit result data that police determine may be evidence in an active investigation of a specific case, then the change may be a positive one," the ACLU wrote in an analysis of the new policy. "But if 'Evidence Mode' triggers the retention of any ALPR data that is searched, then the new mode could indefinitely retain all the ALPR data Flock collects and shares nationally."
Broadly, many of Flock's new safety features have not been proven to prevent pervasive law enforcement misuse, the ACLU argues: "Transforming an exceptionally dangerous mass surveillance system into one that is fully protective of civil rights and civil liberties is a difficult, if not impossible task."
Why are Flock cameras controversial?
In the last month, communities have rallied to "deFlock" their neighborhoods, including destroying, blocking, and even stealing Flock cameras installed there. Many city governments, and even fellow tech companies, have canceled contracts with the company, as others debate continued partnerships.
To many, the "eye-in-the-sky" Flock camera has become a looming symbol of tech-enabled state surveillance and unfettered data collection. As of June, the company operates more than 120,000 cameras in 6,000 different neighborhoods, used across a gamut of businesses, law enforcement agencies, and even homeowner associations to monitor anyone who happens to drive by.
For years, privacy experts and civil rights advocates have raised alarms over the escalation of automated license plate reader (ALPR) systems across the country, as well as the covert nature of ALPR surveillance hardware in public spaces. Flock to update software to prevent police misuse as OKC weighs camera contract
As law enforcement agencies across the nation, including in Oklahoma, consider their use of controversial license plate readers, a leading company behind the technology says a new update aims to crack down on police officers who misuse the data.
The update, which was announced on Thursday, Aug. 13, after a slew of high-profile cases that allege misuse of the system, will crack down on police officers who misuse the data the cameras gather.
Some of these misuses include police officers running searches not tied to law enforcement investigations, including to stalk or harass someone.
The move comes at the same time that leaders in Oklahoma City are considering whether the city would renew its contract with Flock Safety to continue operating the nearly 300 Automate License Plate Reader cameras in the Oklahoma City metro. The item has appeared on several city council meeting agendas in recent months but has been pushed back each time.
City councilmembers have heard concerns from both residents and some council members themselves about a deal and what that would look like in Oklahoma City.
Flock cameras have been used in the city since 2022.
Councilmember Camal Pennington, representing Ward 7, previously said his main concerns are having a thorough system to monitor and trace officer searches while also ensuring city data is not a part of a nationwide database but only shared with local jurisdictions.
Flock has been facing mounting pushback from citizens across the political spectrum over privacy, along with instances of vandalism and protest by those who oppose how ubiquitous the cameras have become across the United States.
Critics have sprawling concerns about privacy and surveillance, but Flock is focusing on officers who misuse data in this new update.
In an interview with USA TODAY, CEO Garrett Langley saidFlock Safety is taking a stand against police abuse of power and for the privacy that everyday citizens expect. New measures rolling out on Aug. 13 will help put a stop to police misusing the system, and send up flags for any attempted misuse, he said.
"You will get caught," Langley said in a message to law enforcement seeking to use Flock for personal gain.
The company's cameras are installed within the jurisdiction of more than 6,000 law enforcement agencies in the country. Flock says it has 120,000 cameras in 49 states.
Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel at the American Civil Liberties Union, previously told USA TODAY that the technology triggers concerns about government overreach on the right, and worries about who is being targeted on the left.
"There's different reasons, but everyone is arriving at the same position, which is mass government surveillance in this country has gotten completely out of control and needs to be reined in immediately," Marlow said.
Meanwhile, the technology has revolutionized the way police track suspected criminals. In July alone, Langley told USA TODAY that the cameras helped solve 1,000 missing person cases and 22,000 stolen vehicle cases.
What are the changes to Flock?
In an announcement on Aug. 13, Flock stated that the original 30-day retention period of all footage will be changed to a 7-day retention period and introduced a new "evidence mode."
The decrease follows after the company saw that over 90% of searches are done within a week, making the 7-day retention the most appropriate time for footage to be kept.
Evidence Mode, however, will address the cases where longer investigations are needed. Using the switch, detectives can preserve specific ALPR data as evidence for an active investigation in cold storage, consistent with existing laws and policies.
Evidence Mode is not yet out but will be rolled out in the coming weeks, Flock Safety said.
The introduction of 7-day retention is not automatically applicable for existing customers. New customers will enroll in a 7-day default, but existing customers can adopt the 7-day recommendation and obtain Evidence Mode.
"Every community will continue to choose the retention period that fits its public safety strategy," Flock Safety said in a statement.
The new update will now require all law enforcement customers to adopt the audit assistance feature, which detects abnormal activity from users. When a user's activity meets the threshold of "abnormal activity," Flock Safety said that they will be locked out and suspended from viewing access.
An administrator will have to review the lockout before reinstating the user in the system.
When asked about the updates to the system, OKCPD officials had yet to review the looming updates and declined to comment.
Councilwoman Hamon speaks on updates
In the past, Councilwoman JoBeth Hamon, representing Ward 6, voted no on an amendment to the contract with Flock Safety, alongside Pennington and Councilman James Cooper, representing Ward 2. With the new changes from Flock, Hamon said her opinion remains unchanged.
"I feel like they could be doing more, and I even feel like other states and cities have gone even further," Hamon told The Oklahoman on Aug. 13. "... It's telling that they could be doing more just as a standard of practice to help protect people's privacy, etc., [but] they just would prefer not to because it's not in their best interest as a company that's trying to make money off a product."
Hamon's concerns remain the network functionality that other agencies can opt to look through and that the technology acts as a threat to individuals' civil rights.
With the new update flagging suspicious activity from officers potentially using the service for personal reasons, Hamon feels it's a better move, but akin to tiptoeing into the correct direction, but not a full step.
She described the database as having "too many side doors" that offer access and being "leaky," even with the accountability the company is trying to build into the tool itself.
Flock isn't the only camera system of its kind, Hamon acknowledges. When asked if there is an alternative to the system that could create the same effect, Hamon said she doesn't have one, but not for lack of research.
"To me, the ALPR technology itself has rot at its core. We value living in a country where we value our freedoms, value our freedom of movement, and have the ability to freely move without the expectation that the government is going to surveil us everywhere we go. No use of this technology is really worth whatever purported benefits that they are reported to have, regardless of whether it's Flock or another company that offers it," Hamon said.
Whether it be the new changes that Flock is set to implement or the contract that Hamon and the remaining councilmembers will be voting on, there isn't a change that can be done on this side of the service that would make Hamon support a new contract.
"It's maybe one thing to have a camera mounted on a public utility pole that's sort of generally capturing a stream of images, which I still have concerns about, but this is the level of searching for individual numbers and attributes of a car," Hamon said.
"That's just another layer of detail that I think is just at its core."
This article contains reporting from Maria Guinnip, The Oklahoman, and Jeanine Stantucci, USA TODAY.

Amid public backlash, Flock announces platform changes
sources.text:
By SARAH RANKIN and CLAUDIA LAUER, Associated Press
RICHMOND, Va. (AP) — Flock Safety, the surveillance technology company increasingly under scrutiny from lawmakers, civil liberties advocates and citizens across the U.S., announced Thursday it is making changes to its platform intended to quell privacy concerns and address documented abuses of its system by some members of law enforcement.
The company is one of the nation’s largest providers of automated license plate readers, which document plate data and other vehicle characteristics as automobiles pass Flock’s cameras. The thousands of law enforcement agencies that contract with the company can search and share that data across jurisdictions to inform investigations.
Police have credited the technology as an important crime-fighting innovation that has helped locate missing people and track suspects in violent crimes. But dozens of cities and agencies have nixed their relationships with Flock amid concerns that the data can be accessed for immigration enforcement or used in unauthorized surveillance, after a flurry of examples surfaced of law enforcement officers misusing the technology for personal searches.
CEO says changes will drive accountability
In an interview, Flock CEO Garrett Langley said many of the product changes will make what were once optional guardrails mandatory for its users to implement by Jan. 1.
Among them: All law enforcement customers will have to implement an audit tool that’s intended to flag abnormal search behavior. When the system detects abnormal behavior, the user would be locked out pending an internal review, the company said in a description of the changes provided ahead of Thursday’s announcement.
Flock, which says its customers own the data that the cameras record, is also shortening the standard data retention window from 30 days to seven. It said it will allow data to be preserved for longer when it is evidence tied to a case number.
Law enforcement users will now also be required to enter a code from their records management system tying each search to a specific case before it is run, something Langley said civil liberties advocates have long been calling for. Overrides for emergencies would be automatically flagged for review, the company said.
Customers will also be allowed to decide which offense types — such as homicide or arson — outside agencies can search their data for, which would allow a customer to block outside searches related to immigration enforcement, the company said.
Langley said that change will give individual cities and departments control to use the system in a manner “consistent with community values.”
Critics say updates still leave room for abuses
Critics of the company reacted skeptically to the changes, which they said appeared designed to address the growing bipartisan anger about the cameras but could still leave room for police to abuse the system.
The American Civil Liberties Union said in a blog post that the shortened evidence retention window could be “a step in the right direction,” but it characterized the other changes as “retreads” of inadequate safety measures.
Robert Frommer, a senior attorney at the Institute for Justice, a public interest law firm that’s led closely watched litigation over the technology, called the changes “window dressing” from a company in “panic mode.”
“This is window dressing that doesn’t address the fundamental problem, which is that police officers are the ones deciding who and when to search, and that should be done by judges with real warrants,” he said.
Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a professor at the George Washington University Law School whose scholarship has focused on policing, big data surveillance and the Fourth Amendment, said he’s been surprised to see the “growing community backlash” against Flock specifically, given the technology is not new and other companies sell it as well.
But Flock and the movement against it have “captured people’s sense that maybe they don’t want to be surveilled all the time,” said Ferguson, a former public defender who earlier this year published a book about policing and surveillance.
More than 50 agencies or jurisdictions canceled, suspended or rejected a contract or deactivated their cameras since the beginning of the year, according to a tracker maintained by DeFlock, a grassroots group formed to track the use of license plate reader technology and push back against it.
In Congress, Republican representatives filed at least two bills aiming to restrict the use of the technology in July.
Ian Adams, an associate professor of criminology at the University of South Carolina currently working on a Flock-related research study, said many of the concerns raised about how the company’s data can be used are not new concerns in law enforcement.
“Anyone with policing experience could have reasonably foreseen that what have been termed as ‘curiosity searches’ by officers, searches for private reasons not related to police work, were going to be a problem this technology faced,” he added, noting that other technologies and platforms like the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information had faced those issues.
Successes and failures have captured attention
Flock, based in Atlanta, Georgia, often posts to its website what the company deems to be everyday examples of success stories for its cameras, including finding missing seniors and catching car thieves. But the tech has also been used in high-profile cases that have garnered national attention, such as the search for a suspect in a fatal shooting at Brown University and in tracking and arresting a former North Carolina police officer who authorities say had made threats that he planned to carry out a mass shooting at a festival in Louisiana.
Abuses have also drawn widespread attention. The Washington Post reported earlier this month finding nearly 50 instances of police officers charged or accused of using the cameras for unauthorized purposes, many for tracking current or former romantic partners or family members.
Just this week, six employees — including four officers — of the Savannah Police Department in Georgia were fired after they were accused of searching for friends and family using the tool and allowing an officer from an outside agency to use the city’s cameras.
The Savannah department said it was made aware of the misuse through Flock’s voluntary audit function.
___
Lauer reported from Philadelphia.

sources.news_title: Flock's Cameras Remain Civil Liberties Threat Despite Updates
sources.text:
Despite 'New' Updates, Flock's Creepy Cameras Remain Major Civil Liberties Threat
Surveillance company Flock Safety announced several operational changes in response to a torrent of criticism and overwhelming public opposition to its mass government surveillance product.
Flock’s threat to privacy stems from its operation of more than 120,000 automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) nationwide, which includes broad location data collection and sharing. While one proposed change to Flock’s operations might constitute a positive development, most of the other changes seem to be following Flock’s playbook of treating legitimate privacy concerns as mere public relations problems. Several of the proposed changes Flock is touting are merely retreads of previous inadequate safety measures.
ALPR companies like Flock violate our privacy across the country by taking photos of every vehicle passing their cameras, logging detailed information about them into a massive nationwide database, and making it possible to track those vehicles and apply AI to uncover their occupants’ private patterns of life. The ACLU is fighting alongside communities to cancel local ALPR contracts and push lawmakers to protect our rights from this surveillance nightmare. Below, the ACLU details and responds to Flock’s announced changes.
Flock reduces default data retention time period, but the devil may be in the details.
Flock announced it is reducing its standard data retention from one month to one week, conceding for the first time that “roughly 90 percent of all searches on Flock already happen within a week” of the data’s collection.
“For cases that need more time, Flock is launching Evidence Mode: when a search is tied to a case number, that data is preserved instead of aging out after 7 days,” Flock said in its statement. “Agencies can still set retention to whatever their state or local policy requires. Evidence Mode will be provided to customers at no cost.”
Our Response: While Flock has not shortened the default retention period to the ACLU’s recommended 48 hours, its proposal may be a step in the right direction. Whether this is a real change or just another Flock PR move, however, will depend on how its “Evidence Mode” operates.
If “Evidence Mode” only retains hit result data that police determine may be evidence in an active investigation of a specific case, then the change may be a positive one. But if “Evidence Mode” triggers the retention of any ALPR data that is searched, then the new mode could indefinitely retain all the ALPR data Flock collects and shares nationally. This would make Flock’s data retention problem even worse. Even if “Evidence Mode’s” data retention hold only applies to hits returned on a given search, it would still retain significant amounts of location data on persons and vehicles who law enforcement do not suspect have engaged in any wrongdoing.
While Flock doesn’t establish state or local ALPR data retention periods, its system empowers governments to choose their own retention periods. For states and localities that want and permit longer data retention periods, all they have to do is ask. Although Flock may not technically be the one unlocking the door to months of people’s private location data, it is responsible for building the door and handing out the keys.
Flock claims to provide more local control over what their ALPR data can be searched for; it has repeatedly failed to effectuate such limitations in the past.
Flock claims that its changes will provide “more local control,” meaning local police can decide what types of offenses other Flock customers can search their data for. “For example,” Flock said, “City A could allow City B to search its cameras for a stolen vehicle or violent crime while blocking searches related to immigration enforcement.”
Our Response: This is not new. Flock has attempted this before, and the security measure failed because users were easily able to circumvent the system’s requirement that police input the purpose of their search.
For example, on June 12, 2025 Flock started claiming its new “Proactive Search Term Tool” would block any “impermissible” searches, such as abortion-related searches in states like Illinois that prohibit sharing reproductive healthcare data. But police officers quickly realized they could just input “investigation” or even “hehehe” as a search reason and it would be approved. Flock later switched from an open text box to a drop-down menu of reasons, but that just offered police a list of acceptable purposes they could choose from, whether it was accurate or not. Until Flock demonstrates they can develop a reliable, workable system to prevent improper searches, this promise of local control provides nothing more than a false sense of security.
Flock claims the universal roll out of its audit assistance tool will detect police misuse, but the effectiveness of its audit tool has never been independently evaluated.
Flock’s next change makes its “Audit Assistance” tool, which the company claims “flags abnormal search behavior,” a standard feature for all its customers. Flock lauds the effectiveness of its audit tool by simply stating that “identification of [police officer] misuse went up” after it established its audit tool.
Our Response: While providing “Audit Assistance” to all departments makes sense, there is no evidence that the tool works consistently to address what the Washington Post observed is a growing pattern of police officers turning Flock into a personal stalking tool. While dozens of officers have recently been arrested, fired, or otherwise disciplined for misusing Flock for personal reasons, Flock claims these arrests are proof its auditing tool works. However, unless we know the number of officers misusing the system, we cannot conclude if Flock and its auditing tools are catching 95 percent of violators or 5 percent. Flock needs to have its auditing tool analyzed by an independent evaluator to determine its actual effectiveness. Until then, we don’t know if the tool is a real security measure or just window dressing.
Flock claims requiring the reasons for a search will prevent abuse, even though that same intervention failed miserably before.
Perhaps the oddest part of Flock’s announcement is its claims that “now every search will require” police to input a case code, a previously optional requirement it first rolled out in July 2025. While claiming that a “search without a reason is a search that shouldn’t happen in the first place,” Flock’s announcement fails to note how easily users have circumvented “search reason” security measures in the past or how its new policy improves the quality of the feature. This leaves the public wondering how making an ineffective voluntary security measure mandatory will improve its functionality.
Our Response: Until Flock demonstrates through independent evaluation that its search reason requirement is an effective, air-tight security measure, it’s reasonable to assume its past failures are prologue.
Transforming an exceptionally dangerous mass surveillance system into one that is fully protective of civil rights and civil liberties is a difficult, if not impossible task. That is even more the case with a company like Flock, whose nearly $1 billion in venture capitalist funding has locked it into an operational model that seeks to trade our privacy for massive profits. Given that Flock’s latest announcement still appears more focused on addressing a perceived PR problem than the significant harms its products create, this is hardly the step forward Flock wants us to think it is. Change may still come as Flock faces this ever growing threat to its corporate viability, and we will continue to analyze the company’s proposals fairly and honestly, but we certainly won’t be holding our breath.

sources.news_title: Flock rolls out new police auditing and accountability controls following surveillance concerns
sources.text:
Law enforcement technology company Flock introduced new safety controls on Thursday, hoping to curb growing scrutiny and fears around surveillance and police misuse of its tools.
Flock’s nationwide network of automated license plate readers (ALPR) cameras —mounted along public roads — take images of passing vehicles’ plates, color and other characteristics to feed into a database. Police departments contract with the company to search the database, billed as a tool to help solve crimes.
But a string of recent police officer resignations or arrests for alleged abuses of Flock’s license plate reader camera system, including to stalk exes or romantic interests, have added to nationwide concerns among privacy advocates and community members about the technology. Some cities have cancelled their Flock contracts, and some critics have gone so far as to vandalize the cameras.
Flock CEO Garrett Langley was motivated to update Flock’s safety controls after realizing just how many people lack trust in law enforcement.
“I’ve spent a lot of time in the last two years talking to individuals, and a lot of them have said, ‘Well, I don’t trust the police,’ and I go, ‘Why?’ ‘Oh, well, the police have abused their power so many times,’” Langley said in an interview ahead of the announcement. “What’s changed for me is realizing that we have a responsibility, maybe an obligation even, to the communities we serve to set the standard.”
Flock is now requiring all customers to use its “Audit Assistance” tool by the end of this year. The tool flags abnormal search behavior — for example, by an individual officer. The tool could help address misuse like, for example, the former Milwaukee police officer who court documents show secretly used Flock to search the location of his romantic partner 124 times.
When the system detects unusual searches, the user will be locked out of the system pending an administrator review, according to Flock.
The company says that around a third of its agency customers turned on the Audit Assistance before it became mandatory.
“This is designed to intervene before misuse becomes recurring or widespread, rather than simply documenting misuse after the fact,” the company said in a statement.
The company will also require users to input a case number to justify each search, with the exception of “genuine emergencies” that will be automatically flagged for review, Flock says. This feature was previously optional for police departments, and Flock says it must be turned on for all agencies by the end of this year.
Flock is reducing its standard data retention policy from 30 days — a length of time that the ACLU and others had raised concerns about — to seven days. However, agencies can adjust that retention period based on state or local policy, the company said. It’s also adding an “evidence mode” feature that will allow agencies to preserve data longer than the retention policy allows when a search is tied to a specific case number.
And the company will give local jurisdictions the option to limit how outside agencies can search data from their cameras; for example, allowing searches related to theft but not to immigration enforcement.
Langley called the misuse of Flock cameras by police officers “completely unacceptable,” adding that building guardrails in the technology can help address surveillance concerns.
While the company’s updates are intended to address potential misuse, Langley said he’d also like to see state regulators mandate more accountability from police. He suggested requiring audits and tools to detect unusual behavior across all technology used by law enforcement and harsher penalties for abuses of power.
Rebuilding trust in the company’s products — and in law enforcement’s responsible use of them — may be crucial for Flock’s business. Some cities that canceled contracts with Flock have recently inked deals with competitor Axon.
“Our customers are the community,” Langley said. “Police might pay the bills. Police might make the decisions, but our customer is the community, because that’s who actually receives the benefit of the product.”
CNN’s Eric Levenson and T.M. Brown contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Surveillance company Flock moves to increase oversight after police misuse
sources.text:
Flock Safety, the police tech company that tracks Americans’ vehicle movements through a line of cameras, announced Thursday that it would implement several new safeguards to its products.
The changes that Flock outlined include shrinking the period for how long it holds people’s movement data by default, going from one month to one week, the company said in a news release. In cases where an officer wants to hold data longer, they will be prompted to enter a case number.
To address potential police abuse of Flock’s data on people, the company also plans to fully deploy a system it began testing earlier this year, called Audit Assistance, that will lock out a user whose searches display “abnormal activity,” the release said.
A spokesperson told NBC News that the changes are meant to help address privacy concerns and to stem officer abuse of the cameras, which have prompted some cities to cancel their Flock contracts amid a national wave of vandalism against them. But the American Civil Liberties Union, a long-standing Flock critic, downplayed the new changes as minor.
“My biggest concern was and will continue to be that they are a mass surveillance company that collects billions and billions of license plate scans every month on people who have done nothing wrong,” said Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel at the ACLU.
Flock makes a range of high-tech surveillance products but is best known for its nationwide fleet of automated license plate readers, pole-mounted cameras that log cars as they pass popular roads and intersections, creating a massive database of each car’s movement, license plate number, make and model, and time of travel.
While the system has been championed by many police forces, privacy concerns have grown. Law enforcement offices that contract with Flock do not need a warrant to access travel information and can opt to share their data with local law enforcement offices, statewide or nationwide, creating a database of Americans’ real-time movements accessible to a range of police officers that spans much of the country.
Flock and law enforcement officers who rely on the technology say that it can be an invaluable tool for tracking suspects and can save policing hours. But privacy advocates say that the cameras sweep up unwitting Americans into a giant dragnet, and police officers have been repeatedly accused of stalking people with the technology.
Marlow said that while he welcomed Flock’s shortening its default data retention time (a week is still short of the ACLU’s recommended 48 hours), the company’s proposed reforms did little to address his concerns with license plate tracking.
“Flock collects location data on virtually every car in America every month and then facilitates the nationwide sharing of that data where it can be used to target members of vulnerable and disfavored communities and to undermine the privacy and chill the behavior of everyone in America,” Marlow said.

Flock Safety is slashing how long its license-plate cameras store data from 30 days to just seven — while forcing cops to justify every search — amid mounting scrutiny from privacy advocates and politicians.
CEO Garrett Langley told The California Post the overhaul amounts to the toughest license-plate-reader policy in the country. About 90% of investigative searches on Flock’s system already occur within seven days, Langley said.
“I’ve realized communities need my help,” Langley said, explaining the company’s decision to move beyond simply giving police departments privacy tools and instead make some safeguards mandatory.
“They need flock to set the standard for how this kind of technology should be deployed,” he added. “I think sadly, police abuse has been a problem for longer than people want to talk about.”
The changes come as Flock faces growing criticism over the spread of its automated license plate readers, which can capture information about vehicles traveling through communities and make it searchable by law enforcement.
The American Civil Liberties Union has accused Flock and other ALPR companies of helping create a nationwide mass-surveillance network, arguing that the technology can reveal where people live, work, worship and travel. The ACLU says Flock cameras number roughly 120,000 nationwide.

“The ACLU has pushed for case code as a requirement in the search for years. We built it,” the leading executive of Flock said in announcing the change. “So things like case code, things like audit assistance, those are gonna be hard requirements now.”

The company is also making its Audit Assistance system mandatory for law enforcement customers.
The tool looks for unusual search activity and flags potentially problematic behavior. Flock said roughly one-third of agencies had voluntarily activated the feature after it was introduced earlier this year — and that identifying misuse increased when agencies did so.

Langley said the goal is to catch potential misconduct before it becomes widespread rather than simply documenting it after the fact.
“The solution is not to remove the tools they need to do their job, the solution is to hold them accountable,” he said. “Not enough cities are running audits. Not enough cities are actually checking what’s happening. So we’re just gonna force it.”
Flock is also introducing Evidence Mode, allowing information connected to a case number to be preserved rather than automatically disappearing after seven days. Agencies can also establish longer retention periods when required by state or local law.
Langley said the seven-day figure was chosen after analyzing how quickly investigators typically search the system.
He acknowledged that some people may argue for an even shorter window.
“You could argue it should be 48 hours,” he said. “And that would mean that maybe 50% of crime gets solved. And in seven days, you’re at 90%.”
The changes also come as California lawmakers consider new statewide rules governing ALPR technology.
Senate Bill 1013, authored by state Sen. Sabrina Cervantes, would require public agencies using license-plate readers to train officers, maintain search logs, undergo annual audits and delete data after 30 days unless it is connected to an active criminal investigation. The measure has passed the state Senate and is now before the Assembly.
As flock strengthens its standards around data security, the company is facing one of its biggest political challenge in Los Angeles.
Mayor Karen Bass recently called for an end to LAPD’s contract with Flock, saying the company had lost the trust of Angelenos.

“LAPD owns the data, they always have. LAPD controls who has access to it, not Flock. So it was definitely disappointing to see her say that,” he said.
Flock maintains it has reached out to Bass’ office and is working to schedule a meeting with the mayor.
Langley also questioned why Bass’ position had changed.
“What’s changed?” he said, pointing to previous support for the technology. “I’ve been running the same business for nine years.”
Bass’ office did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.
Langley said the company remains optimistic about working with LAPD and stressed that the department’s contract has no monetary value to Flock.
“The contract is really clear,” Langley said. “The customer owns the data, not Flock.”
Langley also pointed to Flock’s response to the devastating Palisades Fire, saying the company donated more than 50 cameras to the affected community and that the technology helped produce recoveries.
“Thousands of officers were relying on Flock every single day,” he said of LAPD. “Today, they have nothing.”
Langley said he hopes the department ultimately reinstates the system with the new safeguards in place.
“My team has [spoken with LAPD],” he said. “I think they’re going to be quite happy with these changes.”
The privacy debate is unlikely to disappear.
The ACLU argues that ALPR systems can track innocent drivers and have been misused by law enforcement, while police agencies say the technology helps them recover stolen vehicles, identify suspects and solve crimes.
Langley says the company is willing to keep tightening the rules as the technology improves.

Millions of Americans are being watched as the US ramps up mass surveillance with help from AI, data brokers, and partnerships with private tech companies.
Government surveillance isn’t new, but new wide-ranging technologies that can detect our faces and track our movements are making it more ubiquitous. While the tools have changed, the purpose remains the same: to chill independent thought, free speech, and dissent, bringing our country closer to 1984.
Millions of Americans are being watched as the US ramps up mass surveillance with help from AI, data brokers, and partnerships with private tech companies. Immigrants, people seeking reproductive healthcare, and activists are among the most intensely monitored, but tech like Flock cameras has brought the issue into communities across the country.
According to the American Civil Liberties Union, police departments have increasingly deployed automated license plate readers (ALPRs) powered by AI to track drivers “without a warrant, probable cause, or even reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing.” And they’re doing this with little to no oversight or regulation. 
Flock Safety is one of the largest ALPR vendors in the US. Their solar-powered, teardrop-shaped cameras capture images of all passing vehicles, storing the car’s make, model, and other identifying features. Any law enforcement agency with a Flock contract can access the company’s nationwide database without a warrant.
As more communities wake up to the danger, the solution isn’t trading one brand of camera for another.
Flock cameras also track people. Their “FreeForm search” feature has allowed police departments to search the database using phrases like “male with tattoos” and “person on skateboard,” according to data reviewed by 404 Media.
DeFlock, an open-source project that maps license plate readers, has identified over 128,000 ALPRs in the US. Even my small town of around 20,000 people in Southern California has at least 35 ALPRs, most of them Flock cameras.
No independent research has shown that ALPRs can reduce crime. But there’s mounting evidence of the technology’s alarmingly high error rate. An analysis by the Roseville, California police department found that 71% of Flock’s alerts to the Roseville police incorrectly flagged vehicles as stolen or used in a felony.
Far from promoting “public safety,” the tech has led to wrongful arrests, profiling, and countless other abuses.
Flock reportedly has shared license plate data with federal authorities, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Among other cities, Los Angeles recently suspended their use of Flock cameras amid mounting privacy concerns over who controls the data and how it’s shared.
Court records obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation show that Texas deputies searched 83,000 Flock cameras nationwide to track a Texas woman across state lines because she allegedly “had an abortion.” In Dunwoody, Georgia, a public records request revealed Flock employees accessing cameras in children’s spaces at a community center as part of sales demonstrations.
Other reporting has found cops repeatedly misusing the Flock system to stalk exes.
More communities are organizing and fighting back against this unregulated AI technology. As a result, at least 100 cities have now rejected ALPRs, most of them Flock cameras. But Flock is only one cog in the machine. Cities can easily replace their Flock cameras with those from competitors like Axon, Motorola Solutions, or Genetec, as some have already done.
Mass surveillance remains the fundamental problem. Ever more companies collect our data through cellular networks, facial recognition, surveillance cameras, and ALPRs, among other sources.
The US government, in turn, purchases massive amounts of our data from commercial data brokers without obtaining warrants—bypassing our Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable searches and seizures. In tandem, multiple federal agencies now have sweeping access to Americans’ sensitive personal data through systems built by Big Tech company Palantir, following President Donald Trump’s 2025 executive order that expanded data sharing across agencies.
This metastasizing mass surveillance state—what George Orwell called “Big Brother” in 1984—is eroding our privacy, freedom, and Constitution.

WASHINGTON (TNND) — Flock Safety says it will require new anti-abuse safeguards across its license-plate-reader network after investigations found widespread police misuse, including officers accused of using the system for personal surveillance.

Flock will also deploy its automated auditing system across all law-enforcement customers to flag unusual searches. The company’s auditing system had previously been enabled by only about one-third of agencies using the platform.
The reforms follow reporting that officers have used plate-reader systems to track romantic interests. The Washington Post identified at least 50 officers accused, charged or convicted of misusing Flock or other plate-reader systems, including officers tracking girlfriends, ex-wives and other romantic interests, and later confirmed more than a dozen additional cases. Recent allegations have also surfaced in Georgia, North Carolina and Arizona.

Agencies will be able to preserve information connected to active investigations through a new “Evidence Mode” and, with governing-body approval, adopt longer retention periods.
Police departments will also gain more control over cross-agency searches. Agencies will be able to specify which categories of investigations outside departments can use their camera data for, such as allowing searches involving homicide or kidnapping while blocking searches related to immigration enforcement.
The changes amount to making previously optional safeguards mandatory. CEO Garrett Langley said the company had expected state and local governments to mandate stronger controls themselves but decided it needed to act faster. Flock says its network includes roughly 120,000 cameras and produces about 20 billion plate scans per month.
Critics say the safeguards address obvious vulnerabilities but do not resolve broader concerns about surveillance. Civil-liberties and policing experts have welcomed measures such as case-number requirements and shorter retention, while arguing that protections should be imposed by law rather than left to a private vendor. Others have questioned whether AI-based auditing can reliably detect misconduct or substitute for independent human oversight.

Flock is tightening its rules in response to a growing surveillance backlash
The company is imposing new guardrails on its police tech after reports that officers are abusing it and cities are dropping contracts. But the changes leave glaring loopholes.
The police-tech giant Flock is announcing today that it will change officers’ access to its nationwide network of license plate readers, in an apparent effort to quell a growing backlash and win back contracts lost amid concerns about mass surveillance and police abuse.
Several changes aim directly at a problem that has made recent headlines: officers abusing Flock’s technology to stalk and harass current or former romantic partners. Flock’s 120,000 cameras form a nationwide network that police departments can use, giving officers access to an enormous pool of searchable location data. A recent Washington Post investigation found 46 cases in which officers were accused of using Flock's cameras for unauthorized purposes like stalking.
To combat that, the company will start requiring officers to enter a criminal case number before conducting a search. The system was launched as an option last year but is now required. It’s meant to verify that each search has a legitimate purpose.
This is a baseline standard that civil liberties groups have asked for, but officers have found ways around similar safeguards. The ACLU recently found that when Flock required officers to enter a reason for a search, some used generic terms like “investigation” or mocked the prompt entirely; at one Oregon department, officers entered “hehehe” 20 times. Because Flock won’t verify case numbers, officers could circumvent the new safeguard just as easily.
But Flock is now expanding an automatic auditing system that is supposed to catch those who try that, the firm announced today. The feature analyzes officer search activity and flags to administrators anyone with suspicious searches. This was also introduced as an option last year but is now mandatory. Flock has not shared specifics on how accurate the automatic auditing tool is, nor opened it up to independent evaluators.
Beyond trying to prevent officer abuse, Flock is making changes meant to address broader backlash about how much data its network collects and who can search it. The company now recommends that agencies hold onto data for seven days rather than 30 (though they can choose to overrule this). Departments can also now limit other departments’ searches of data from their cameras to those made for certain stated reasons; for example, they might allow investigations related to “kidnapping” but not for purposes of “immigration enforcement.” It’s another safeguard that depends on officers to accurately report why they’re conducting a search.
The changes come as a backlash against Flock has started to come from all angles. Tucker Carlson has said its technology is contributing to a “slave state.” Some cities have reportedly dropped Flock contracts because of such protest, though it’s difficult to estimate how many: In February, NPR found that at least 30 cities had dropped in the last year, but the activist group DeFlock puts the number higher. Some states or municipalities are passing laws to ban license plate readers altogether, while some that allow them are switching away from Flock to the other industry leaders, Axon and Motorola. Flock has said these cancellations represent a small number of the 5,000 agencies that have contracted with the company.
Chad Marlow, a senior policy counsel at the ACLU who has become a sort of nemesis to Flock and other companies making automatic license plate readers, says the backlash is driven less by individual abuses—though those don’t help—than by the sheer scale of surveillance that Flock’s cameras enable.
“In America, you only get to investigate someone if you think they’ve done something wrong,” Marlow says. As license plate readers grow more ubiquitous, officers have increasing latitude to investigate people without first establishing suspicion of a crime, since searching the troves of data the readers collect does not require a warrant. He adds, “Is it worth it to catch a certain number of criminals, return a certain number of stolen cars, to eviscerate Americans’ privacy?”
Flock CEO Garrett Langley traces the backlash to a different issue. “If you look at the main reason we’ve lost customers, it’s misinformation,” Langley told MIT Technology Review. He says people mistakenly believe Flock does facial recognition or sells the data it collects to commercial buyers. (The misinformation charge cuts both ways, however; the ACLU and other critics have published accounts of the company repeatedly lying to city councils and other decision-makers about what its technology can do.)
Though the company has taken steps in response to public concerns, “our change in stance is more of one from building things that are optional,” Langley says, to “building more confidence that as a technology company we have a responsibility to enforce guardrails, not provide optionality.”
Flock’s new rules are undeniably small and incremental compared with what the ACLU has advocated. Marlow is broadly supportive of them but notes that judging whether they reduce abuse would require the company to open its systems to independent researchers for the first time rather than citing internal studies.
More broadly, though, he says the backlash is putting the company at a crossroads.
“Flock has come to the table because this incredible, unprecedented nationwide uprising against their company has scared them,” Marlow says. “But at the same time, they are just absolutely unwilling to make the actual changes they need to make in order to legitimately respond to these concerns. So this is the best that the company is willing to do.”

sources.news_title: Flock license plate readers raise privacy concerns while helping cops
sources.text:
Flock license plate readers are in use in southeast Louisiana, raising privacy concerns while helping cops
Flock license plate readers, a surveillance tool used to identify vehicles, help police in southeast Louisiana solve crimes while sparking concerns about privacy and misuse.
Kenner police Chief Keith Conley said the city installed more than 50 Flock cameras in 2023 and now has over 70. The department recently used the system to arrest a man driving a stolen car, according to a Facebook post.
"We put them up [in 2023], and within three or four months we had already solved a first-degree murder," Conley said.
Kenner police used to have about a dozen license plate readers before switching to the Flock system. Conley said the other cameras relied on electricity and would often be out of service. So, they switched to Flock because those cameras are solar-powered and maintained by the company.
Conley said the Flock license plate readers alert officers if a car in the National Crime Information Center database is photographed in their city. Other than that, he said Kenner cops can only search for pictures of cars related to a specific case.
"It is a vehicle recognition camera," Conley said. "You can put any kind of description of a vehicle, a bumper sticker, any unique feature of that vehicle, and it will search the system and find it."
Kenner’s subscription to Flock costs about $250,000 annually, funded by the state. That total includes the cost of the equipment and maintenance.
"So far this year we've probably solved 100 or more cases, everything from hit-and-runs to protective orders to stolen vehicles," Conley said.
Flock’s website states its cameras are used in more than 12,000 communities across the U.S.
"If a detective puts in a vehicle that's wanted for a certain crime, you know, it'll hit any Flock system that's throughout this region, throughout this country," Conley said.
While law enforcement officials praise the technology, others express concerns about its implications for privacy. As WDSU's sister news station in Orlando, Florida reports, some police in that region have taken their license plate readers offline.
"It's not just about keeping track of one person. It's everybody in the country, every man, woman and child in a vehicle," said civil rights attorney Glenn McGovern.
McGovern said Flock is different from other license plate readers because it collects nationwide data on cars and their movements.
"We're past 1984. This is worse," McGovern said, referencing George Orwell’s dystopian novel. "There are no [federal] standards, and each municipality has to come up with their own standards, and they're behind the ball on this."
Earlier this month, The Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers nationwide have been charged with misusing Flock cameras or similar systems, sometimes to stalk people, including former romantic partners.
"The things that can go wrong are terrible," McGovern said.
He told WDSU he is also concerned about bad actors potentially hacking into Flock's database.
Conley said Flock searches are internally checked by higher-ranking police personnel to help prevent misuse of the system's data in Kenner.
"We have access to a lot of criminal databases," Conley said. "That kind of abuse can take place in those systems as well. So I would never punish the whole city of Kenner if I find one officer abusing the system; I'm just going to get rid of that officer."
Flock’s website states that its license plate readers do not identify people and the system tracks who searches for what. However, the company’s video cameras — a separate product — detect human presence, but not personal characteristics.
Flock did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday.

sources.news_title: Flock tightens guardrails aimed at stopping cops from abusing its license plate cameras
sources.text:
The News
Following revelations that rogue police officers used car-tracking software from Flock Safety as a tool for stalking, the $8.4 billion startup said Thursday it planned to roll out new measures to prevent abuse of its license plate camera data.
The Atlanta-based company, which was founded in 2017 and has deployed more than 120,000 cameras around the US, is making the changes after The Washington Post reported this month that police officers have used its technology to stalk women with no connection to any investigations. It fueled broader concerns over the constant surveillance the cameras afford and fears over the data reaching federal immigration officials, reigniting debates over what constitutes public safety. Dozens of Flock cameras across the country have been targeted and destroyed.
Flock is shortening its standard data retention period from 30 days to seven, cutting how far back anyone could retrace a car’s movements. The company will also flag abnormal searches from within police departments, locking out those users and alerting their managers. And officers won’t be able to run a search for license plate data without having a case number attached to the query.
“We’ve listened,” Garrett Langley told Semafor, adding that communities “have a higher expectation of Flock than maybe even I was holding us to.”
Know More
The additional safeguards still leave gaps, in part because police departments aren’t Flock’s only customers: Businesses and homeowner associations can also buy the cameras — giving private citizens more tools to investigate crimes that happen in their community, but also opening up more opportunities for abuse, often with less oversight.
Langley said that he wanted to fight back against a “misconception that we are some evil entity that has these diabolical plans… the reality is we just want people to be safe.”

sources.news_title: Harvey expands police surveillance network with Flock camera technology amid privacy concerns
sources.text:
HARVEY, Ill. (WLS) -- While some cities are canceling contracts with police surveillance giant Flock, the south suburban city of Harvey is embracing it.
Harvey law enforcement gave the ABC7 I-Team the first look at its new real-time crime system, demonstrating how the suite of surveillance technology works. Officials said it is helping improve public safety and emergency response, while critics continue to raise concerns about privacy and the potential for misuse.
Inside the slick new center police demonstrated how it was used it to search for a downed power line following storms earlier this week. Police Chief Dale Mitchell said the drone has been used alongside the fire department and public works crews to identify hazardous conditions, including flooding, fallen trees and damaged electrical lines.
"We had a series of recent storms and the cameras and the drone was used to look for those unsafe areas, flooding streets that were impassable, trees that were down, electrical lines that were down, where if we were just trying to use city personnel, it would take us a lot longer time, maybe hours and hours, whereas we can use our network of cameras and the drone to search those areas for those dangerous conditions," Mitchell said.
Harvey's real-time crime center includes live video cameras with pan, tilt and zoom capabilities, automatic license plate readers, gunshot detection technology and a semi-autonomous drone. The integrated surveillance network is powered by Flock and covers the city of about 20,000 residents.
Mayor Shirley Drewenski said the system has applications beyond policing.
"The real time Crime center is not only based on crime, but also our personal safety. This unit is used through the fire department, our street department," Drewenski said.
Mitchell said the technology is intended to monitor locations rather than individuals.
"I want to stress, we're watching places. We're not watching people. And we can't watch every camera all the time. We focus our attention on those people that have committed a crime," he said.
Harvey officials said the city is the first in Illinois to receive a Flock Safe City designation and has deployed nearly every surveillance product offered by the company, funded through grants.
Asked whether the technology has reduced crime, Mitchell said, "The data shows that we've seen a reduction in crime. ... one of the biggest benefits of this technology. It reduces the time for when we respond, and it reduces the time from recognizing those conditions that are unsafe."
Police said reductions have been seen in several crime categories, including robberies and homicides. Mitchell also confirmed that Flock technology has been used in the investigation of a double homicide last month that remains unsolved.
Police also said traffic citations have increased.
Real-Time Crime Center Director Cameron Biddings said the technology improves situational awareness for officers.
"It's been very beneficial. We'll be able to survey the land, be able to see what's going on, give that information in real time to our officers in our dispatch center and be able to have them respond accordingly," Biddings said.
RELATED | Raging debate around use of license plate readers: Are they advancing safety or violating privacy?
The expansion comes as privacy advocates continue to question the growing use of police surveillance technology. Critics have raised concerns about the ability to track people's movements without a warrant and about the possibility of misidentification through video analytics and license plate reader systems.
According to Harvey police, live video feeds and license plate reader data are retained for 30 days unless connected to an ongoing investigation. Police also have the ability to search live and recorded video using identifiable characteristics, such as clothing color or whether someone is carrying a backpack.
Beryl Lipton, senior investigative researcher with the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital rights nonprofit, said questions remain about the reliability and oversight of the technology.
"How often are people misidentified and charged with crimes they didn't commit or are now subject to a criminal investigation because video analysis surfaced them in one of these platforms," Lipton said.
She is imploring community members to get involved in the conversations about the trade-offs between public safety and the right to privacy and she joins of chorus of other privacy advocates calling for better transparency and oversight.
"What communities should continue to expect is that is access to some of these transparency portals or to some of the oversight mechanisms that have been put into place," Lipton said. "I think it remains incredibly important that law enforcement is transparent about the way that they're deploying these tools."
Flock has also faced scrutiny elsewhere. The I-Team reported that Los Angeles paused its contract with the company over vehicle misidentification concerns involving automatic license plate readers. The report also noted that officers in multiple jurisdictions have been disciplined for alleged misuse of Flock technology and that some cameras have been vandalized, including incidents that led to charges against three men in DuPage County.
Flock spokesman Paris Lewbel said the company has added new safeguards designed to detect improper use.
"Earlier this year, we built our audit assistance, or we released audit assistance tool that automatically flags any suspicious searches to command staff so they can conduct an investigation," Lewbel said.
He said vandalized cameras can affect investigations.
"Every time a camera is damaged, it means that camera's going offline. And that means that has an impact on the local police department being able to use it as part of an investigation," Lewbel said.
Harvey police are aware of the privacy concerns and insist the technology is largely intended to help identify criminal activity, locate suspects and eliminate innocent people from investigations.
"We're not looking for anybody individually unless they've committed a crime or they're committing some type of act that's unsafe," Mitchell said.
Harvey police declined to disclose the number of cameras installed throughout the city but said the city owns all of its data and that it cannot be shared or used without permission. Flock told the I-Team that it does not use facial recognition technology and has no such technology currently in development.

sources.news_title: Op-Ed: The Fight Against Flock Cameras Is Just the Beginning
sources.text:
Op-Ed: The Fight Against Flock Cameras Is Just the Beginning
Government surveillance isn’t new, but new wide-ranging technologies that can detect our faces and track our movements are making it more ubiquitous. While the tools have changed, the purpose remains the same: to chill independent thought, free speech, and dissent, bringing our country closer to 1984.
Millions of Americans are being watched as the U.S. ramps up mass surveillance with help from AI, data brokers, and partnerships with private tech companies. Immigrants, people seeking reproductive health care, and activists are among the most intensely monitored, but tech like Flock cameras has brought the issue into communities across the country.
According to the ACLU, police departments have increasingly deployed automated license plate readers (ALPRs) powered by AI to track drivers “without a warrant, probable cause, or even reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing.” And they’re doing this with little to no oversight or regulation. 
 
Flock Safety is one of the largest ALPR vendors in the U.S. Their solar-powered, teardrop-shaped cameras capture images of all passing vehicles, storing the car’s make, model, and other identifying features. Any law enforcement agency with a Flock contract can access the company’s nationwide database without a warrant.
Flock cameras also track people. Their “FreeForm search” feature has allowed police departments to search the database using phrases like “male with tattoos” and “person on skateboard,” according to data reviewed by 404 Media.
DeFlock, an open-source project that maps license plate readers, has identified over 128,000 ALPRs in the U.S. Even my small town of around 20,000 people in Southern California has at least 35 ALPRs, most of them Flock cameras.
No independent research has shown that ALPRs can reduce crime. But there’s mounting evidence of the technology’s alarmingly high error rate. An analysis by the Roseville, California police department found that 71 percent of Flock’s alerts to the Roseville police incorrectly flagged vehicles as stolen or used in a felony.
Far from promoting “public safety,” the tech has led to wrongful arrests, profiling, and countless other abuses.
Flock reportedly has shared license plate data with federal authorities, including ICE. Among other cities, Los Angeles recently suspended their use of Flock cameras amid mounting privacy concerns over who controls the data and how it’s shared.
Court records obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation show that Texas deputies searched 83,000 Flock cameras nationwide to track a Texas woman across state lines because she allegedly “had an abortion.” In Dunwoody, Georgia, a public records request revealed Flock employees accessing cameras in children’s spaces at a community center as part of sales demonstrations.
Other reporting has found cops repeatedly misusing the Flock system to stalk exes.
More communities are organizing and fighting back against this unregulated AI technology. As a result, at least 100 cities have now rejected ALPRs, most of them Flock cameras. But Flock is only one cog in the machine. Cities can easily replace their Flock cameras with those from competitors like Axon, Motorola Solutions, or Genetec, as some have already done.
Mass surveillance remains the fundamental problem. Ever more companies collect our data through cellular networks, facial recognition, surveillance cameras, and ALPRs, among other sources.
The U.S. government, in turn, purchases massive amounts of our data from commercial data brokers without obtaining warrants — bypassing our Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable searches and seizures. In tandem, multiple federal agencies now have sweeping access to Americans’ sensitive personal data through systems built by Big Tech company Palantir, following President Trump’s 2025 executive order that expanded data sharing across agencies.
This metastasizing mass surveillance state — what George Orwell called “Big Brother” in 1984 — is eroding our privacy, freedom, and Constitution.
As more communities wake up to the danger, the solution isn’t trading one brand of camera for another. We need oversight and regulation of the entire surveillance industry, as well as the government agencies that rely on it.
