sources.news_title: Flock CEO Touts Company’s Commitment to Public Safety Amid Public Backlash
sources.text:
DETROIT ~ Amid growing backlash against automated license plate readers (ALPRs), the CEO of one of the key makers of these camera systems wants to reassure the public that its systems are about public safety and not violating privacy.
Flock Safety is the leading producer of ALPRs, which capture photos of license plates and vehicle details of cars on roadways, parking lots, and shared access points. Simultaneously, the cameras also record data about the location, date, and time a vehicle’s image was captured, according to Flock’s website. These cameras are used primarily by local governments and police departments in criminal investigations to flag vehicles of interest, though reassurances from the company on data collection have not cooled concerns from privacy activists over the proliferation of these cameras.
VIDEO:
Aug. 12, 2026 ~ Garrett Langley, CEO of Flock Safety, joins Kevin Dietz in studio to discuss the technology helping law enforcement agencies solve crimes, improve public safety, and address privacy concerns surrounding surveillance systems.
“I started this company nine years ago, (and I) just wanted to live in a safer neighborhood,” Langley told WJR. “I live in Atlanta, and I didn’t understand why this would be so valuable. I didn’t realize that 70% of crime starts with a car, ends with a car.“
While he said that facial recognition is not part of Flock’s uses and only records vehicle information, organizations like the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) have raised concerns about mass surveillance, arguing that ALPRs can be used to invade people’s private lives by tracking them from houses of worship, protests, medical centers, and more. The organization has been pushing back against ALPRs at the local and state levels across the country by engaging with local activists, pushing to retract existing Flock contracts, and potentially banning the use of ALPRs altogether or getting governments to adopt guardrails on ALPR data sharing and retention.
“It is hard to roll out 120,000 ALPR cameras and counting and not have the public notice,” Chad A. Marlow, senior policy counsel at the ACLU, told WJR. “Once the public noticed, their objections were loud, relentless, and effective – not to mention entirely non-partisan. In truth, we’d have the same pushback against all other government mass surveillance techs if they were as easy to notice as Flock ALPRs.“
The backlash against Flock over the past year has manifested into acts of vandalism and destruction, including a recent incident from Winona, MN, where someone cut down and stole all eight of the Flock cameras in the town. City council meetings across the country have been swarmed with residents pushing back against contracts for ALPRs in their communities, including in Michigan. So far, the cities of Ferndale, Bay City, and Westland have either failed to pass contracts with Flock or cancelled them.
While there are no official counts of ALPRs installed in the U.S., the volunteer-based activist group DeFlock gathers user-submitted information on where they have been installed and maps them out for people to see where they have been put up in their communities. According to their database, over 100,000 have been put up nationwide and over 3,000 in Michigan. Langley estimates that a third of the state’s communities use Flock cameras.
Langley said that concerns over privacy are “real” and has worked to address these concerns with local communities. He said he had a conversation with a mayor in Michigan about using Flock systems in their town, and reminded them that the city can set how long the pictures can be stored. He added that pictures are typically stored for 7 to 30 days and are permanently deleted if they are not used in investigations.
“Read our contracts. We got 7,000 cities under contract, and they all say the same thing: our customers own the data. Our customers can control it,” Langley said. “But we got to do a better job explaining how this system works.“
Another point of concern surrounding Flock surveillance systems has been the abuse of the system by some police officers across the country. A Washington Post report found at least 50 known cases of police officers who have used Flock cameras to track and stalk exes, romantic partners, or other women, including a case from Georgia where a deputy was fired and arrested for using Flock cameras to track someone he was in a “personal relationship” with.
Marlow said that other government systems have been misused in the past by police and claims that Flock has accountability checks built into their systems to detect these abuses. However, Marlow said that when “privacy is traded for profits,” abuses of this type of system are inevitable.
“While police officer abuse of the Flock system was inevitable and is deeply regrettable, the bad acts of a couple dozen or even hundreds of irresponsible cops are not nearly on the same level of eviscerating the privacy of 350 million Americans,” he said. “The police cases do further demonstrate that Flock’s mass data collection and sharing business model creates unacceptable risks and that Flock is incapable of controlling.“
Langley, though, maintains that ALPR technology is an effective tool for law enforcement, claiming that Flock helped find 10,000 missing people. He added that the system can ping vehicles associated with a felony warrant, a missing child, or an Amber alert.
“It’s a balance,” Langley said. “If we stored this data forever, we’d solve more crimes, but I think we all feel that feels wrong. We probably shouldn’t store where people go, where they drive by, forever. So we said 30 days is a pretty good thing. Now, what we believe is I shouldn’t make that decision. State regulators should, and so in nine states this year, they’ve made decisions that roughly 21 days is a better balance of both efficacy and privacy.“
However, Marlow said that opposition to Flock and mass surveillance is not about hiding bad conduct; it is to do with maintaining privacy and avoiding a chilling effect on the exercise of any person’s freedoms. For instance, he argued that someone struggling with alcoholism may skip Alcoholics Anonymous meetings if they don’t want to be tracked to these meetings and reveal private information about themselves.
“When people are being tracked all the time, it impacts their sense of privacy, freedom and chills the exercise of their rights,” he said. “Worse still, if we don’t draw the line here, mass government surveillance and privacy intrusions will only continue to get worse.“

sources.news_title: Flock Cameras Are Supposed to Fight Crime Not Track Weed
sources.text:
Flock cameras were supposed to help police catch criminals. Instead, a growing number of cases show the technology being used to monitor perfectly ordinary Americans
Flock cameras were sold to police departments as a powerful new weapon against crime. The pitch was simple: Use license-plate cameras to find stolen cars, identify suspects and help solve burglaries, assaults and murders. The public was sold Flock cameras are supposed to fight crime not track weed….so how did it go wrong?
The question is emerging as Flock Safety’s nationwide network of automated license-plate readers expands. The cameras can record where vehicles are seen and allow law enforcement agencies to search the information later.
A recent Wisconsin case shows how far the power can reach.
Police used Flock data to track a Wisconsin man who repeatedly drove to Michigan, where recreational marijuana is legal. His travel pattern became part of an investigation ultimately leading to police to stopping him over suspected marijuana possession.
RELATED: New York and Texas Take Opposite Paths on Cannabis, CBD and Hemp
Think about the resources involved. A camera records a license plate. Someone searches the database. Investigators analyze travel patterns. Officers follow up and make a traffic stop. Prosecutors may ultimately become involved.
All because a driver went to a state where marijuana is legally sold.
Flock does not publish a universal price for its cameras, but public contracts and reporting have put the cost at roughly $2,500 per camera annually, depending on the agreement. For a department with 100 cameras, that can mean roughly $250,000 a year before considering the personnel time required to investigate the information those cameras produce.
That’s a lot of technology and police resources.
The question is whether those resources are being directed at the crimes Americans actually expect police to prioritize.
How many burglaries were solved with those cameras? How many stolen cars were recovered? How many violent offenders were identified? How many murder investigations benefited? And how much time was spent looking for people suspected of buying weed?
The issue isn’t Flock cameras are inherently bad. Used to find a violent criminal or recover a stolen vehicle, they can be enormously valuable.
The concern is a small number of government officials appear willing to use the technology to enforce a broader idea of how citizens should live.
This concern became even more striking in Texas, where investigators used the Flock network to search for a woman who had obtained an abortion. Records obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation showed that the search reached more than 83,000 cameras.
Flock can help police catch criminals. But a nationwide system capable of tracking where Americans drive can also become something else: a tool for monitoring personal behavior.

sources.news_title: Letter: What’s Wrong With Flock? The Perils of Quiet Mass Surveillance
sources.text:
Letter: What’s Wrong With Flock? The Perils of Quiet Mass Surveillance
Welcome to our letters to the editor/opinion section. To submit yours for consideration, please send to [email protected]. Please consider including an image to be used–either a photograph of you or something applicable to the letter. However, an image is not necessary for publication.
Remember opinions expressed do not necessarily reflect that of Redheaded Blackbelt nor have we checked the letters for accuracy.
Across America, from tiny rural towns to major cities, cameras called Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) are stationed at key intersections, gathering information from every vehicle that passes by. Each camera is part of a huge network, and each image is added to a centralized searchable database.
The Ukiah Police Department has 14 of these cameras. They don’t just catch people who run red lights. Flock Safety’s technology just starts with the license plate. When there’s a network of cameras, the combined data clearly shows the travel history of a vehicle. AI-driven data analysis reveals its traffic patterns, predicts where it is likely to go, and can reveal all visitors to a given location. It can be used to target drivers who attend protests, health clinics, centers of worship or other sensitive locations.
In addition to capturing license plate data, the photographs can reveal images of the vehicle, the vehicle’s drivers and passengers and even people getting in and out of a vehicle.
When law enforcement agencies, prompted with scripts from Flock Safety, cite individual examples of major crimes solved in order to argue that mass surveillance is an important tool, they ignore that it’s a convenient shortcut around due process. For serious crimes, police have always had a standard legal process that includes making the case to a judge on why they should get a search warrant for location data, whether it’s from cell phones or service providers. Police treat ALPR databases as if no legal threshold exists, giving them free rein to track a person’s movements without any judicial oversight.
Is any of this legal?
The Flock system and all similar ALPRs track the movements of each person who passes them. The Supreme Court has stated in two cases, (United States v. Jones, and Carpenter v. United States) that our expectations of privacy include privacy of our physical movements.
In Carpenter v. United States the Supreme Court rejected the argument that venturing into public eliminates Fourth Amendment protection. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that the government’s access to 127 days of cell-site location data, tracking movements on public roads, achieved near perfect surveillance, as if it had attached an ankle monitor to the phone’s user. The Court made this clear: “A person does not surrender all Fourth Amendment protection by venturing into the public sphere.” While they haven’t ruled on ALPR data, the parallels in terms of warrantless dragnet data collection are unmistakable.
Here in California, under  Senate Bill 34, state law enforcement agencies are barred from sharing license plate reader data with out-of-state public agencies or federal entities. The law has been routinely violated; civil liberties groups in 2023 found that 71 California law enforcement agencies had broken it. Later that year, Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an advisory providing police with specific guidance on how to comply with the law.
So there are a couple of issues: First, public record reviews show that most law enforcement agencies within California contract with each other to share their data, so if even one agency is willfully violating California law, it opens what’s called a “side door” access for the Federal government to see everybody else’s data. 
Second, earlier this year Flock conveniently changed their search request options to remove any mention of ICE or immigration. Instead the drop-down menu for the purpose of searches is “investigation” or “criminal justice.”
California sanctuary laws bar police from assisting in immigration enforcement, and another law prohibits sharing data from automated license-plate readers with out-of-state cops for any purpose. Still, ICE has persuaded local law enforcement officers to run searches for them through Flock Safety’s entire network of data. CBP, including Border Patrol, also operates a network of covert ALPR systems in many areas.
An analysis of 10 months of searches on Flock Safety’s servers by Electronic Frontier Foundation found that over 50 agencies ran hundreds of searches through Flock’s national network targeting protest activity. These searches included activities related to the 50501 protests in February 2025, the Hands Off protests in April 2025, and the No Kings protests in June and October of 2025. During 2025 many officers probed the nationwide network with terms like “protest” without articulating an actual crime under investigation.
Flock recently changed how one initiates a search on their platform. All an officer has to do now is claim an investigation. Since earlier this year, audits of Flock data simply won’t capture any kind of surveillance targeting at-risk communities or political free speech activity.
Flock made at least four changes to its standard Terms and Conditions (T&C) under the latest contract, dated Feb. 16, 2026. According to an April 2026 article by the ACLU, the changes include:
Sale of data. Flock’s previous T&C stated that “Flock does not own and shall not sell Customer Data.” That language has been removed.
A perpetual license. The T&C now adds a “perpetual” right for Flock to use customer data to “support and improve” its services — this lets them keep using surveillance data even after the customer has terminated its contract and can’t access it anymore.
Liability, termination, and arbitration provisions. The new contract expands Flock’s protections against liability, potentially shifting liability costs to taxpayers. The risk of financial liability led Mountain View, CA to terminate its Flock contract.
What about Ukiah?
Ukiah states that its public-facing transparency page shows just a few hundred searches per month of its Flock cameras. But this number accounts only for the searches conducted by the Ukiah Police Department.
According to department records that were provided in a public records request, data from Ukiah’s Flock cameras was searched over 10 million times in 2025. Only 11,000 of these searches were by UPD. The rest were done by other law enforcement agencies.
10 million searches a year is over 27,000 searches daily, over 1,100 searches of our local database every hour of every day, mostly by “partner” agencies over whom we have no control.
According to UPD Chief Tom Corning, every search has a case number and is checked for appropriateness. Yet all partners have to do is report an “investigation” to access Ukiah’s data. With search terms like “investigation” and 1,100 searches every hour, it’s impossible for anyone to decipher if any given access is legal or necessary.
City staff assure us data is only retained for 30 days. If your movements are tracked as part of those 1,100 hourly searches, it doesn’t take 30 days to get a picture of your activities. And they can keep tracking you on day 31.
Ukiah spends $35,000 a year of taxpayer money on a system that effectively shares everyone’s movements 24/7 with a lot of outside agencies. Is this loss of privacy even cost-effective?
According to Mayor Susan Sher at a City Council meeting, using the cameras led to 110 arrests during a four-year period.
The only year for which we were given complete data is 2025, when the Ukiah PD searched the camera data 11,128 times. Extrapolating over a four-year period, that’s over 44,000 searches by the UPD, yielding 110 arrests at a total cost of $140,000.
There are no guardrails to Flock
Cornerstones of the American legal system have always included the right to due process and the right of privacy. On both national and local levels, this translates into laws, policies, and procedures that balance the needs of public safety with the individual rights of people to move freely about in the world and for people to assemble peaceably free from surveillance.
Law enforcement officers and prosecutors have always had a standard legal process for obtaining judicial permission to step past the boundaries and obtain warrants, whether to arrest, to search, or nowadays to get cell phone or email information.
The ability of any random police officer to enter the Flock database, instigating searches across not just local data but data from hundreds of “partners” and with just the vaguest of search terms, is an utter debasement of our legal system norms.
Mass surveillance by Big Brother was at one time in the realm of dystopian science fiction.
It’s here now, and we were never even asked for permission to submit to this attack on our basic civil and human rights.

sources.news_title: Navajo Nation Deploys Flock Cameras While Other Governments Pull Back
sources.text:
The Navajo Nation is turning to Flock Safety to help tackle crime despite privacy concerns by other governments.
America’s largest Native American reservation will deploy Flock Safety’s license plate reader cameras to help cover the 27,000-square-mile reservation that spans Arizona, New Mexico and Utah.
“The Navajo Nation faces some of the most difficult public safety challenges in the country, and [the cameras] will be a force multiplier for the Navajo Nation,” said Courtney Terlecki, a spokeswoman for Flock Safety, said in a written statement. We’re proud to stand with the [Navajo Department of Criminal Investigations] and [Navajo Police Department] to help close that gap.”
As the Navajo Nation is using Flock Safety cameras to assist with law enforcement, other parts of Arizona are pushing back against them.
Katelynn Contreras, a policy strategist for the American Civil Liberties Union of Arizona, told The Center Square this week that “people are worried about how their privacy is being violated.”
“People are becoming more aware around the pervasiveness of how this technology is being used and how data is being collected,” she said.
Navajo authorities face unique challenges.
According to the Navajo Police Department, the nation has “over 205 commissioned officers and over 100 civilian support staff, including police dispatchers,” serving a population of more than 178,000 people.
The Center Square reached out to the Navajo Police Department, but did not hear back before publication time.
Terlecki said that Flock Safety cameras “help law enforcement investigate and solve cases including stolen vehicles, burglaries, assaults, missing persons and other serious crimes.”
Terlecki said law enforcement agencies “can also receive real-time alerts on license plates tied to stolen vehicles, wanted suspects, or missing persons cases such as AMBER and Silver Alerts, which helps officers locate vehicles faster, close cases sooner, and recover victims and property.”
Terlecki said Flock Safety last year “supported more than 1 million criminal investigations and incidents, assisted an estimated 20% of solved cases in jurisdictions where its technology is deployed, and helped locate more than 10,000 missing persons.”
Canceling contracts
“Flock is building a nationwide mass surveillance system piece by piece with municipalities, grid companies, homeowner associations and other various government entities,” Contreras said.
She added that these cameras are a “flagrant violation of [people’s] right to privacy,” which is protected by the Fourth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution and Article 2, Section 8 of the Arizona Constitution.
Contreras said this section of the Arizona Constitution gives residents “greater protection from unwanted government snooping.”
No state regulations
Arizona does not currently have any state law that regulates Flock or other automatic license plate reader technology, she noted.
Terlecki said over “40 courts across the country have determined that fixed license plate readers do not violate the Fourth Amendment and cannot track the whole of an individual’s movements.”

Flock Cameras Spark Community Backlash

“If you haven’t done anything wrong, you’ve got nothing to worry about.” That is the mantra of those who believe surveillance technology is a public benefit. The UK has perhaps the largest number of security cameras per capita of any nation, and its citizens seem to be perfectly happy knowing they are being observed every moment of every day while outdoors. But surveillance has a potentially darker side. In the late 1800’s, Jeremy Bentham proposed a way to control prisoners by housing them in a a circular structure he called a Panopticon.
The guards would be located in a central area, with the prison cells arranged around them. This would allow the guards to observe the prisoners every moment of the day. Because the prisoners would never know when they were being watched, they would voluntarily refrain from inappropriate behavior, which in turn would allow the prison to operate with fewer guards than would otherwise be needed.
Flock License Plate Reading Cameras
In 2020, a company by the name of Flock Security started installing small license plate tracking cameras in certain neighborhoods. It’s business proposition was simple. It marketed itself to police departments by claiming its cameras could help them find stolen cars, locate wanted people, and solve crimes.
Today, Flock Safety is valued at more than $8 billion and has about 120,000 cameras installed throughout the United States. It has contracts with 40 percent of all police departments in the US. It has become the digital equivalent of Bentham’s Panopticon, although in this case it is not just prisoners who are under surveillance, it is the entire population.
Danielle Citron, a professor of law at the University of Virginia, told the New York Times recently, “We all expect and deserve privacy. The problem is that we typically cannot feel, see, or experience the loss as it is happening. Seeing those cameras is a punch in the gut. We see them and it says you have no room to just be, to go about your day feeling lost in the crowd.”
Flock And The Fourth Amendment
The right of privacy, although recognized in most countries, is not specifically set forth in the US Constitution. The closest the US gets to it is the Fourth Amendment, which says, “The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.”
Millions of words have been written about what is or isn’t a permissible intrusion by the government into private lives and it is fair to say that the question is far from settled. According to USCourts.gov, “Whether a particular type of search is considered reasonable in the eyes of the law, is determined by balancing two important interests. On one side of the scale is the intrusion on an individual’s Fourth Amendment rights. On the other side of the scale are legitimate government interests, such as public safety. The extent to which an individual is protected by the Fourth Amendment depends, in part, on the location of the search or seizure.”
Antonin Scalia is considered one of the most notable conservative Supreme Court judges ever. You might think he would be a fierce supporter of the ability of the police to pursue law and order goals. But in fact, in the case of Kyollo Vs. US in 2001, he voted to invalidate a conviction of a marijuana grower. In that case, the police used a thermo imaging camera to determine the attic of the defendant’s home was unusually hot.
They raided the home and found an array of “grow lights” being used to cultivate marijuana. “Grow lights” give off a lot of heat and that heat is what the cameras outside the house detected. Scalia ruled the police needed to obtain a warrant before searching the home — much to the surprise of Scalia’s most ardent supporters.
The Danger Of Surveillance
What many do not realize is that all 120,000+ Flock license plate reading cameras are linked together in a nationwide database. Those with access to that database know which hot sheet motel a philandering spouse is frequenting. who we meet with. and who is slipping across a state border to seek reproductive health services. In Texas, where 700 Flock cameras are now in operation., concerns about the cameras have united both progressives and conservatives in an unlikely coalition that opposes adding more cameras and wants those already installed removed.
Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio recently suspended their contracts with Flock to prevent immigration authorities from accessing data from the cameras. Dayton resorted to covering the cameras with trash bags. In cities like Houston, Oakland, California, and Grand Junction, Colorado, residents have taken matters into their own hands, with police reports and surveillance footage documenting Flock cameras being cut down, splattered with paint, and even being disabled by gunfire.
Knoxville County mayor Glenn Jacobs told NewsNation in an interview, “They’re just collecting data as an active surveillance system, and every car that passes through, the data is collected from that car license plate, using AI. They make a vehicle fingerprint of the car that includes distinguishing features, make, model, color, bumper stickers, roof racks, all these different things. They’re just pulling everything in. And then it’s retained for sometimes 30 days or more in a searchable database.”
Action & Reaction
The founder of Flock Safety is Garrett Langley, who told The Hill that his surveillance equipment manufacturing company started out because of his frustration with crime rates in his home city of Atlanta. “Crime felt too easy to get away with,” Langley said during a TED talk in April. “It didn’t make sense that you could steal someone’s car … or you could kill someone and have a 50 percent chance of getting away with it. … So I did what engineers do. I built a license plate-reading camera.”
For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. In this case, that reaction takes the firm of DeFlock, an organization whose mission it to raise awareness about automatic license plate readers and “the threats they pose to personal privacy and civil liberties.” On its website, people can search for known Flock camera locations in their area. “Camera locations come from volunteers and the OpenStreetMap community, not a private company or government agency,” DeFlock says. Naturally, it has an app that people can download.
DeFlock was started by Will Freeman in 2024. He now lives in Boulder, Colorado, where he the local police department for any information it had collected about him using Flock cameras. The police refused his request, saying “there is no reasonable expectation of privacy on publicly owned streets and sidewalks.” Freeman filed suit to force the department to release the data he requested and called the Flock system a “warrantless surveillance dragnet.” He told the New York Times, “It feels bad to always be watched and scrutinized.”
The ACLU has gotten into the act with a campaign it calls “What The Flock!” On its website, it says, “We have already seen how this mass surveillance tool can be weaponized and abused by law enforcement. ICE and CBP have repeatedly used Flock to go after immigrants without warrants. Kansas police used them to pursue a man who wrote a critical op-ed about the department, while a Colorado police officer wrongfully accused a woman of theft based on a Flock hit and then refused to look at evidence proving her innocence. A mother and her children were held at gunpoint because ALPR cameras wrongly flagged their car as stolen.”
Setting Social Boundaries
The old adage that “If you haven’t done anything wrong, you’ve got nothing to worry about” trips easily off the tongue, but it is of little use when a law enforcement officer is pointing a loaded weapon at you and telling you to get on the ground. Langley says, “It’s going to be an ongoing debate probably forever. We should have this debate and we should continue to evolve our point of view as a society of what we’re comfortable with and what level of safety we want.” It’s possible the issue could make its way to the Supreme Court eventually.
Texas Congressman Keith Self, a Republican whose district is north of Dallas, has introduced a bill that would require federal law enforcement agencies to obtain a warrant before accessing or querying data collected by state and local surveillance systems, license plate readers among them. Somewhere, Antonin Scalia is smiling.

sources.news_title: Flock Camera Systems May Face a Constitutional Reckoning
Atlanta police auditing use of Flock license plate reader system
sources.text:
Atlanta police auditing use of Flock license plate reader system
ATLANTA - The Atlanta Police Department is conducting an audit to determine whether any employees improperly accessed or misused the Flock license plate reader system.
What we know:
APD said officials are reviewing use of the technology to determine whether any officers or other employees accessed the system for personal reasons.
Flock's automated license plate reader technology uses cameras to capture information about passing vehicles, including license plates. The system can be used by law enforcement agencies to search for vehicles and track where particular license plates have been detected.
What we don't know:
Deputy Chief Jason Smith could not provide the number of officers under investigation or state when findings will be released. Department officials declined an interview request, posting online that they value public trust but providing few specific details about the ongoing probe.
When asked by Councilmember Antonio Lewis if the results would be made public, Smith stated he could not speak to future disclosures while the investigation remains active. Officials have not provided a definitive timeline for when the department's review will conclude.
Why APD is reviewing the system
Why you should care:
The Atlanta audit comes after more than a dozen law enforcement officers around Georgia were arrested for allegedly illegally accessing the Flock system.
APD has not said whether it has identified any employees suspected of improper use or how long the department's audit is expected to take.
OTHER RECENT STORIES
Flock cameras used across the country
Big picture view:
According to Flock, nearly 100,000 cameras are deployed in more than 6,000 communities across 49 states.
Law enforcement agencies use the technology to help locate stolen vehicles, identify vehicles connected to crimes and assist with investigations. However, the ability to search license plate information and review where vehicles have been detected has also raised questions about access, oversight and potential misuse.
Across the country, at least 50 officers have been flagged, fired and charged over license plate camera misuse. At least a dozen of those cases occurred in Georgia, including three Bibb County deputies charged recently and three Coweta County Sheriff's employees who resigned under scrutiny.

sources.news_title: Flock cameras may be getting closer look in Park Ridge
sources.text:
In July, Park Ridge aldermen approved a yearlong contract with Flock Group, a Georgia-based company that provides license plate readers to police departments across the country. The contract, for eight cameras, is worth $24,000.
Now, weeks after the contract, one alderman — who was absent for the July vote — said he’d like to revisit the agreement.
The company — and supporters of the company — argue the cameras provide a powerful tool for law enforcement as it allows police departments to track stolen vehicles or missing or wanted persons across a city and even into other jurisdictions. The tool seems almost magic — search for a wanted license plate and find the vehicle in real time.
But over the past year, civil rights advocates have pushed back, arguing that giving a private company real-time data about the movement of every private car in these networks invites widespread abuse. Even people never accused, let alone charged with anything, have been victims of harassment as police and other agencies have misused the camera network. Plus, the company stands accused of violating Illinois state law by illegally sharing license plate data with the Border Patrol.
Consequently, popular opinion — even within local city hall chambers — is shifting. Last year, Evanston and Oak Park killed their Flock contracts while Arlington Heights this year approved a new contract but with penalties embedded in it should Flock misuse local data. Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss said there’s growing local pushback to Flock.
“When I talk with mayors across the country, there’s widespread concern about this,” he said.
At the Aug. 3 Park Ridge city council meeting, Alderperson John Moran made a motion for the Flock camera contract to be brought back for debate. Moran wasn’t present for the July vote, but even that vote was opposed by another alderperson, Fred Sanchez, and one member of the community spoke out publicly against the new contract.
Moran’s August motion failed 3-3, and he said afterward he has no plans to revisit the debate until the contract ends. But he did say he does expect some sharp scrutiny next year when the contract renews. He said he’s gotten e-mails and even letters from constituents who are unhappy with Flock.
Moran said, simply, times are different than they were two years ago, when the city first got involved with the company.
“I think that Flock, when it came to us a year ago now, it was at a time when the biggest concern in Park Ridge was property crime,” he said. The biggest property crime was vehicle theft.
But that wasn’t just Park Ridge. In the years following the pandemic, vehicle thefts surged nationally but have fallen in the last two years. This year, the Oak Brook-based National Insurance Crime Bureau reported that since 2024, there has been “a 23 % decrease” in car thefts, and this is “a clear signal of the end of the pandemic-fueled surge in vehicle thefts.”
Another factor the NICB pointed to is that auto manufacturers, namely Kia, updated car software that left certain models particularly vulnerable to thefts. Kia installed free auto immobilizers in 2023 after a popular social media trend highlighted gaps in Kia’s theft prevention.
But even as car thefts declined everywhere, Flock abuse reports began creeping up.
In 2025, a Texas sheriff’s officer searched the database of 83,000 cameras across the nation, including some in Illinois, to search for a woman who’d left that state to get an abortion. Abortions aren’t legal in Texas, but they are in Illinois. Also in 2025, the Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias announced Flock was illegally handing over Illinois data to immigration officials. Both violations happened two years after the state passed a law that prohibited unauthorized data sharing over state lines. The state issued the company a warning, and Giannoulias has since asked local authorities to double-check their agreements with Flock to make sure those agreements don’t violate state law.
Moran said that’s exactly what he did — he read the agreement. And, he said, in his opinion it comes very close to violating the law.
For example, he said there’s language in the contract that “exonerates Flock if they do anything that might be seen as outside of the contract.”
Indeed, on page 18 of a 20-page contract, Flock says they’ll hand over data to any outside authority if “legally compelled” and they’ll provide Park Ridge with a timely notice.
In addition, he said there’s a clause that promises they delete the data, but there’s another clause that says they will hand over the camera data — including deleted data — if required by a court.
“Those two statements seem to run contrary to each other. Are they deleted, or not?” he asked.
All of that is cause for concern for Moran.
“My concern now is, what was presented to us as a wonderful new advancement in policing, the negative side of that is showing,” he said. “There’s some unintended uses and unintended consequences of signing up with Flock.”
Moran also pointed out there are at least three apps — FlockHopper, DeFlock and Flock Alert — that alert drivers to the camera locations, allowing for easy bypass.
But even without apps, local car thefts are following national trends, and they seem to be on the decline.
According to the state police uniform crime reporting data, from 2024 to 2025, motor vehicle theft fell by over 20 % in Cook County and the most populous city, Chicago, has never used Flock cameras.
There is no publicly available data yet for the period in which Evanston cancelled their Flock contract. But Biss said he’s not heard any complaints about a lack of Flock protection.
“I’ve heard only positive feedback, and I’ve heard a lot of it,” he said.
Jesse Wright is a freelance reporter for Pioneer Press.

sources.news_title: Flock Cameras Spark Privacy Debate As Network Expands
sources.text:
A crowdsourced map tracking the locations of Flock Safety's automated license plate reader cameras across the United States has drawn renewed attention this week to the rapid expansion of a surveillance network that now spans more than 5,000 law enforcement agencies and 6,000 communities nationwide, reigniting a long-running debate over the balance between public safety and privacy.
Flock Safety, an Atlanta-based company founded in 2017 and valued at $7.5 billion after a $275 million funding round earlier this year, operates what the company describes as the country's largest network of automated license plate readers, with more than 120,000 cameras installed across 49 states. The cameras use artificial intelligence to photograph passing vehicles and log identifying details — including license plate numbers, vehicle make, model, color and features such as bumper stickers or roof racks — into a searchable database that participating law enforcement agencies can access, typically retaining the data for 30 days or longer depending on local policy.
Law enforcement officials say the technology has proven valuable in solving crimes, particularly stolen-vehicle cases, missing-persons searches and investigations involving suspect vehicles. Police used Flock cameras last year to help track down the suspect in a mass shooting at Brown University, and the company has publicized cases in which its cameras helped officers locate an abducted toddler and track suspects across multiple counties. "This is such a powerful tool, we don't want to reduce the efficacy of the 99.99% of officers who go to work every single day and want to do good for their community," Flock co-founder Garrett Langley has said in defending the system's overall record.
Civil liberties advocates, however, argue the network functions as a de facto nationwide surveillance system operating with limited oversight. The American Civil Liberties Union has campaigned against the cameras, warning that the technology "records and tracks every car that comes into view" and can reveal sensitive details about a person's life, including which doctors they visit, which religious services they attend or which protests they participate in. Knox County, Tennessee, Mayor Glenn Jacobs described the system in similar terms, telling NewsNation that Flock cameras create a searchable "vehicle fingerprint" for every car that passes, regardless of whether that vehicle is connected to any investigation.
Those concerns have been reinforced by documented cases of misuse. A CNN investigation published last month found that a detective in one department was arrested after admitting to using the Flock system to track two people without a legitimate investigative basis and secretly installing a GPS tracker on one person's vehicle. Separate research has found that Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection have accessed Flock data to pursue immigration enforcement in some cases, and privacy researchers in Washington state identified at least eight local law enforcement agencies that enabled direct data-sharing with Border Patrol during 2025. Advocacy groups have separately raised concerns that the same tracking capability could be used to monitor people traveling to reproductive health clinics in states with abortion restrictions.
Flock has said its cameras do not use facial recognition and are not designed for general surveillance, positioning the technology instead as an investigative tool restricted to specific criminal cases, missing-persons searches and public-safety alerts. Some local governments have nonetheless scaled back their use of the systems over cost or oversight concerns; the city of Greenfield, Massachusetts, announced plans earlier this year to remove its four Flock cameras after determining it could no longer afford to maintain them, even as police there credited the cameras with aiding several investigations, including a murder case and a bank theft.
The debate over Flock's rapid growth is likely to intensify as more communities weigh whether to adopt or expand the technology, particularly given the absence of comprehensive federal regulation governing how license-plate data can be collected, shared or retained. Whether individual states or Congress move to impose new limits on automated license plate readers, or whether law enforcement agencies adopt stricter internal policies in response to documented misuse cases, is likely to shape how far the technology's footprint extends in the coming years.

Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-IN) said he’s planning on taking legislative action against Flock Safety cameras after having a personal experience with law enforcement aided by the license plate readers.
“I just don’t like where we’re going with Flock cameras. I think that it’s invasive, as you said. It’s too big government,” Stutzman told the Just the News, No Noise television show on Friday.
“You know the law enforcement folks would argue that they can use these as a tool. You know they can be where you can’t have a human police officer in its place,” he continued.
“For example, I pulled into my driveway, and all of a sudden, a police officer pulls in behind me. I said, you know, ‘Can I help you? Did I do something wrong?’ And he said, ‘Well, your car’s registration has expired,'” Stutzman explained.
“So I looked, and it was in my wife’s name. I somehow missed it. Of course, we got it taken care of. But you know, he recognized my car because the Flock cameras relayed the information that you know we had driven into town, and it was under the jurisdiction of these Flock cameras, and it just, to me, I felt very uneasy about it,” he added.
Stutzman explained that he and other Congress members are discussing legislation to limit the use of the controversial cameras.
“I think that this is a step too far. There has to be boundaries. There have to be controls in place. You know, of course, you can always argue. Well, we’re able to catch the bad guys, but you know what? There’s 95% good people out there doing the right thing. We would have taken care of that registration one way or the other. We didn’t need a police officer following us to our house to remind us,” Stutzman said.
“Several of us are going to start looking at some legislation to rein these in to be sure that it’s not crossing the line and invading people’s privacy,” he added.

“Draconian” – GOP Congressman Wants To “Ban” Flock Safety Cameras
POLITICO has more:
Communities across the U.S. are cutting ties with Flock Safety, one of the country’s leading producers of license plate readers and other surveillance systems, over concerns around mass surveillance and data privacy — and fears over how data could be used in immigration crackdowns.

Residents have swarmed city council meetings in states where Flock cameras have cropped up to urge elected officials to cancel contracts or deactivate Flock cameras — arguing that the technology could be used to track people traveling to places of worship, medical care centers, political protests and other sensitive locations.
“It was a bipartisan issue within our community. We had work boots and Subarus in our parking lot and they were united in their position against the Flock cameras,” Josh Young, a Republican commissioner of Macon County, North Carolina, said in an interview.
Over 20 local jurisdictions either stopped using Flock cameras or began the process of doing so in July, according to a tracker maintained by DeFlock, an activist group that has been mapping the company. It’s the highest amount in a single month since they began tracking in 2021.
The pushback against the surveillance technology — which caught fire in some liberal towns last year amid fears of data collection related to President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown — runs parallel to sprawling fights over the future of technology in American life, including the rise of increasingly advanced artificial intelligence tools and the construction of massive data centers needed to power them.

sources.news_title: An Upper West Side Flock Camera Map Misunderstanding
sources.text:
By Gus Saltonstall
A screenshot of the Upper West Side from a map of Automated License Plate Reader camera locations has received enormous attention online in the past few days.
As you can see from the image, all but one Manhattan neighborhood has multiple dots.
The Upper West Side is empty. It is eye-catching.
The map in question is called DeFlock, which is an open-source, volunteer-powered project for identifying and documenting the locations of automated license plate readers across the United States. The map, which was referenced and linked to in a New York Times article on Tuesday, gets its name from Flock Safety.
Flock Safety is a private company based in Atlanta, Georgia, that creates these automated license plate reader cameras that then use artificial intelligence to identify and track vehicles. The use of the company’s cameras has grown increasingly controversial due to worries about unwanted surveillance and breaches of privacy.
You can read more about the debate surrounding Flock’s cameras — HERE.
But, back to the Upper West Side.
“Odd, there’s not a SINGLE Flock camera on the Upper West Side,” one person wrote on Twitter to the tune of 50,000 likes and 24 million views.
On Reddit, a person penned, “A Map of all the Flock Cameras in the Upper West Side of New York. Not a single one.” The post received more than 3,000 upvotes and over 340 comments.
There are multiple apparent misunderstandings connected to the DeFlock map and screenshot of the Upper West Side that West Side Rag wants to clarify.
The first? The DeFlock map shows locations of all Automated License Plate Reader cameras, not just cameras made by Flock Safety.
The second? There are no Flock Safety cameras in New York City.
The New York Police Department, the New York City Department of Transportation, and the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which all operate or use Automated License Plate Reader cameras in the city, confirmed to West Side Rag on Thursday that they do not hold contracts with Flock Safety.
West Side Rag also clicked through all of the location dots for automated cameras in Manhattan on the DeFlock map to double-check, and found none made by Flock Safety.
Whereas, if you venture out to Kinnelon, New Jersey on the DeFlock map, you find cameras made by Flock.
That being said, the notoriety of Flock Safety has caused many people to mistakenly use the name Flock as a substitute for all Automated License Plate Reader cameras. While there are no Flock cameras in the five boroughs, as anyone who routinely drives knows, there are plenty of Automated License Plate Reader cameras in the city.
The Automated License Plate Reader cameras, sometimes referred to as Red Light cameras, have been used in New York City since 1994. These cameras are operated by the New York City Department of Transportation and are primarily used to catch cars committing traffic infractions.
As stated by DeFlock, its online map tracks all Automated License Plate Reader cameras, not just the automated cameras made by Flock Safety.
Many of the Manhattan Automated License Plate Reader cameras are made by companies such as Ekin Box Spotter or RedSpeed.
The question remains, though. Regardless of which company made the Automated License Plate Reader cameras, why are there none on the Upper West Side on the map?
The answer is that the open-source, volunteer-reliant map is incomplete.
There are plenty of Automated License Plate Reader cameras on the Upper West Side.
The city and police department try to keep the locations of these cameras secret, but law firms such as Weiss & Associates provide a list of where you can find some of them.
There are Automated License Plate Reader cameras at the following Upper West Side locations, according to the law firm.
- West 66th Street and West End Avenue
- West 72nd Street and Central Park West
- West 72nd Street and Amsterdam Avenue
- West 96th Street and Amsterdam Avenue
- West 96th Street and West End Avenue
- West 110th Street and Amsterdam Avenue
The automated cameras also appear in GPS apps such as Waze, and anyone who routinely drives on the Upper West Side could most likely provide a longer list of the camera locations than the one above.
Returning to the viral DeFlock map screenshot of our neighborhood.
For whatever reason, nobody has submitted the locations of the Automated License Plate Reader cameras to the DeFlock map for the Upper West Side, but as shown above, that does not mean they are not there.
Additionally, the red-lined box in the screenshot conveniently includes Central Park, where it makes sense that there aren’t cameras, and does not count the eight Automated License Plate Reader cameras along West 60th Street, which West Side Rag counts as the Upper West Side, connected to the MTA’s congestion pricing program.
If any Upper West Sider has free time, you can submit the locations of the Automated License Plate Reader cameras on the DeFlock map — HERE.

sources.news_title: Flock announces privacy updates to its car-tracking cameras following national criticism
sources.text:
By New York Times
Flock Safety, a company facing increasing scrutiny of its nationwide car-tracking technology, announced several updates on Thursday it said would improve privacy protections and prevent misuse.
The company’s network of 120,000 cameras, which can read license plates, are used by 7,000 law enforcement agencies across the country. Police departments say the systems help solve crimes. But reports of misuse by law enforcement, along with anxiety over the technology’s ability to surveil ordinary people, have led to protests and prompted some cities to end their contracts with the company.
“I realized we had a responsibility to do more,” said Garrett Langley, chief executive of Atlanta-based Flock.
Some cities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, have stopped using Flock cameras in order to prevent immigration authorities from gaining access to their data. To provide more local control, the company said on Thursday, it will allow individual police departments to restrict what other law enforcement agencies can see — allowing access to data to find stolen vehicles, for example, but not for immigration violations, the company said. It also is shortening the default time for data retention to a week, down from 30 days, though departments could change those settings.
Reducing the time that data is retained is a positive development, said Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel from the American Civil Liberties Union. But he noted that it was easy for police departments to keep the data longer.
The heightened local control, too, is “good in theory,” Mr. Marlow said, but has never been proved to work. A similar program was rolled out last year to block impermissible searches, he said, but Flock customers quickly found a workaround.

The current announcement clarified that data will only live on Flock servers for one week. The company announced that the ability for agencies to divide what felonies they want to share data about with other municipalities is another privacy protection concern.

The backlash has been triggered by ongoing reports abusing the technology to stalk romantic partners. Flock’s current series of reforms also intend to prevent abusive technologies.
The company underlined that Flock is making it standard for every law enforcement customer so when a system detects any unusual activity, the user is locked out in real time.
In this connection Flock told Fox Business, “A search without a reason is a search that should not happen in the first place and now Flock’s system automatically treats it that way.”

sources.news_title: Flock announces changes amid backlash over surveillance cameras
sources.text:
Flock Safety, the surveillance technology company increasingly under scrutiny from lawmakers from both parties, civil liberties advocates and citizens across the U.S., announced Thursday that it is making changes to its platform intended to quell privacy concerns and address documented abuses of its system by some members of law enforcement.
The company operates a vast nationwide network of automated cameras that record the license plate numbers and other characteristics of all passing vehicles every day. Thousands of law enforcement agencies in 49 states can search and share Flock’s data across jurisdictions to aid their investigations.
Police have credited the technology as an important crime-fighting innovation that has helped locate missing people and track suspects in violent crimes. But some critics say its pervasiveness amounts to unconstitutional warrantless mass surveillance. Dozens of cities and agencies have nixed their relationships with Flock amid concerns that the data can be accessed for immigration enforcement or used in unauthorized tracking, after a flurry of examples surfaced of law enforcement officers misusing the technology for personal searches.
Flock seeks accountability
In an interview, Flock CEO Garrett Langley said many of the product changes will make what were once optional guardrails mandatory for its users to implement by Jan. 1.
Among them: All law enforcement customers will have to implement an audit tool that’s intended to flag abnormal search behavior. When the system detects abnormal behavior, the user would be locked out pending an internal review, the company said in a description of the changes provided ahead of Thursday’s announcement.
Flock, which says its customers own the data that the cameras record, is also shortening the standard data retention window from 30 days to seven. It said it will allow data to be preserved for longer when it is evidence tied to a case number.
RELATED: #AskJAXTDY | Who’s in charge of Flock cameras in Jacksonville?
Law enforcement users will now also be required to enter a code from their records management system tying each search to a specific case before it is run, something Langley said civil liberties advocates have long been calling for. Overrides for emergencies would be automatically flagged for review, the company said.
Customers will also be allowed to decide which offense types — such as homicide or arson — outside agencies can search their data for, which would allow a customer to block outside searches related to immigration enforcement, the company said.
Langley said that change will give individual cities and departments control to use the system in a manner “consistent with community values.”
Critics skeptical
Critics of the company reacted skeptically to the changes, which they said appeared designed to address the growing bipartisan anger about the cameras but could still leave room for police to abuse the system.
The American Civil Liberties Union said in a blog post that the shortened evidence retention window could be “a step in the right direction,” but it characterized the other changes as “retreads” of inadequate safety measures.
Robert Frommer, a senior attorney at the Institute for Justice, a public interest law firm that’s led closely watched litigation over the technology, called the changes “window dressing” from a company in “panic mode.”
“This is window dressing that doesn’t address the fundamental problem, which is that police officers are the ones deciding who and when to search, and that should be done by judges with real warrants,” he said.
Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a professor at the George Washington University Law School whose scholarship has focused on policing, big data surveillance and the Fourth Amendment, said Thursday’s shifts were “better than the opposite” but called for further scrutiny of the technology in the form of “sustained democratic engagement with the rules and judicial checks on access at a minimum.”
Ferguson said he’s been surprised to see the “growing community backlash” against Flock specifically, given that the technology isn’t new and other companies sell it as well. But Flock and the movement against it have “captured people’s sense that maybe they don’t want to be surveilled all the time,” he said.
More than 50 agencies or jurisdictions have canceled, suspended or rejected a contract or deactivated their cameras since the beginning of the year, according to a tracker maintained by DeFlock, a grassroots group formed to track the use of license plate reader technology and push back against it. Cameras around the country have also been vandalized.
In Congress, Republican representatives filed at least two bills aiming to restrict the use of the technology in July.
Ian Adams, an associate professor of criminology at the University of South Carolina currently working on a Flock-related research study, said many of the concerns raised about how the company’s data can be used are not new concerns in law enforcement.
“Anyone with policing experience could have reasonably foreseen that what have been termed as ‘curiosity searches’ by officers, searches for private reasons not related to police work, were going to be a problem this technology faced,” he added, noting that other technologies and platforms like the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information had faced those issues.
Law enforcement experts said it’s a common tension of “policing in a democracy” — balancing useful technology that officers say helps solve and prevent crime with the community’s interest and right to privacy.
“It’s a balancing act. A community has a legitimate interest in how information is used, but it also has a legitimate interest in the effectiveness of a police department in preventing crime,” said Chuck Wexler, executive director of the Police Executive Research Forum, a Washington-based nonpartisan think tank. “I think a balance can be struck, but it’s more likely to come from department policy than company changes.”
Successes and failures
Flock, based in Atlanta, often posts to its website what the company deems to be everyday examples of success stories for its cameras, including finding missing seniors and catching car thieves. But the tech has also been used in high-profile cases that have garnered national attention, such as the search for a suspect in a fatal shooting at Brown University and in tracking and arresting a former North Carolina police officer who authorities say had made threats that he planned to carry out a mass shooting at a festival in Louisiana.
Abuses have also drawn widespread attention. The Washington Post reported earlier this month finding nearly 50 instances of police officers charged or accused of using the cameras for unauthorized purposes, many for tracking current or former romantic partners or family members.
Just this week, six employees — including four officers — of the Savannah Police Department in Georgia were fired after they were accused of searching for friends and family using the tool and allowing an officer from an outside agency to use the city’s cameras.
The Savannah department said it was made aware of the misuse through Flock’s voluntary audit function.
