sources.news_title: The Fight Against Flock Cameras Is Just the Beginning
sources.text:
Government surveillance isn’t new, but new wide-ranging technologies that can detect our faces and track our movements are making it more ubiquitous. While the tools have changed, the purpose remains the same: to chill independent thought, free speech, and dissent, bringing our country closer to 1984.
Millions of Americans are being watched as the U.S. ramps up mass surveillance with help from AI, data brokers, and partnerships with private tech companies. Immigrants, people seeking reproductive health care, and activists are among the most intensely monitored, but tech like Flock cameras has brought the issue into communities across the country.
According to the ACLU, police departments have increasingly deployed automated license plate readers (ALPRs) powered by AI to track drivers “without a warrant, probable cause, or even reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing.” And they’re doing this with little to no oversight or regulation. 
Flock Safety is one of the largest ALPR vendors in the U.S. Their solar-powered, teardrop-shaped cameras capture images of all passing vehicles, storing the car’s make, model, and other identifying features. Any law enforcement agency with a Flock contract can access the company’s nationwide database without a warrant.
Flock cameras also track people. Their “FreeForm search” feature has allowed police departments to search the database using phrases like “male with tattoos” and “person on skateboard,” according to data reviewed by 404 Media.
DeFlock, an open-source project that maps license plate readers, has identified over 128,000 ALPRs in the U.S. Even my small town of around 20,000 people in Southern California has at least 35 ALPRs, most of them Flock cameras.
No independent research has shown that ALPRs can reduce crime. But there’s mounting evidence of the technology’s alarmingly high error rate. An analysis by the Roseville, California police department found that 71 percent of Flock’s alerts to the Roseville police incorrectly flagged vehicles as stolen or used in a felony.
Far from promoting “public safety,” the tech has led to wrongful arrests, profiling, and countless other abuses.
Flock reportedly has shared license plate data with federal authorities, including ICE. Among other cities, Los Angeles recently suspended their use of Flock cameras amid mounting privacy concerns over who controls the data and how it’s shared.
Court records obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation show that Texas deputies searched 83,000 Flock cameras nationwide to track a Texas woman across state lines because she allegedly “had an abortion.” In Dunwoody, Georgia, a public records request revealed Flock employees accessing cameras in children’s spaces at a community center as part of sales demonstrations.
Other reporting has found cops repeatedly misusing the Flock system to stalk exes.
More communities are organizing and fighting back against this unregulated AI technology. As a result, at least 100 cities have now rejected ALPRs, most of them Flock cameras. But Flock is only one cog in the machine. Cities can easily replace their Flock cameras with those from competitors like Axon, Motorola Solutions, or Genetec, as some have already done.
Mass surveillance remains the fundamental problem. Ever more companies collect our data through cellular networks, facial recognition, surveillance cameras, and ALPRs, among other sources.
The U.S. government, in turn, purchases massive amounts of our data from commercial data brokers without obtaining warrants — bypassing our Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable searches and seizures. In tandem, multiple federal agencies now have sweeping access to Americans’ sensitive personal data through systems built by Big Tech company Palantir, following President Trump’s 2025 executive order that expanded data sharing across agencies.
This metastasizing mass surveillance state — what George Orwell called “Big Brother” in 1984 — is eroding our privacy, freedom, and Constitution.
As more communities wake up to the danger, the solution isn’t trading one brand of camera for another. We need oversight and regulation of the entire surveillance industry, as well as the government agencies that rely on it.

sources.news_title: Cleveland's surveillance debate may grow beyond Flock
sources.text:
Cleveland’s recent debate over surveillance technology centered on license plate readers made by Flock Safety. The next round of the argument could be broader.
Following hours of hearings that featured support from law enforcement and criticism from civil liberties advocates, City Council in July extended Cleveland’s contract with Flock Safety — for another six months.
After that contract runs its course, Mayor Justin Bibb’s administration doesn’t appear ready to walk away from that technology or other forms of electronic surveillance. Last week, City Hall issued a request for proposals to provide Cleveland’s safety forces with license plate readers, gunshot sensors and drones.
Cleveland already uses this technology. But City Council had pressed the administration to seek out bids from more vendors who could offer the services.
Flock isn’t the only company that theoretically could bid on the work. There’s also Axon, the firm formerly known as Taser that supplies Cleveland police with body cameras and the Fusus software platform. Leonardo and Motorola market license plate readers. SoundThinking sells the ShotSpotter gunshot detection system that Cleveland currently uses.
Opponents of license plate readers have focused their attention on Flock, even adopting group names that play off the company’s brand: DeFlock Lakewood, Flock No Cleveland and Shake Off Flock in Shaker Heights.
But if Cleveland swaps vendors, that won’t satisfy those groups’ objections to high-tech license plate readers that photograph passing cars and categorize them in databases using artificial intelligence.
“We see automated license plate technology writ large — and in fact like all AI-powered mass surveillance technology — as a huge problem,” Bryn Adams, a Flock No spokesperson, said in an interview.
With Flock under scrutiny, its competitors may have flown under the radar. That could change.
“It’s awesome that there’s been so much grassroots movement against Flock,” Adams said, “but I think we need to start expanding the conversation and understanding that, you know, this flashy tech startup is just the most visible symptom of a much, much deeper problem.”
Opponents of Flock and license plate readers from Cleveland, Lakewood, Cleveland Heights and Shaker Heights plan a conference this weekend to build support for their efforts.
Council wanted City Hall to cast a wider net for police technology
Council Member Michael Polensek defends license plate readers and has long supported the city’s use of police technology, from body cameras to drones. As chair of council’s Safety Committee, he encouraged the Bibb administration to issue the request for proposals.
Unlike the anti-surveillance activists, Polensek said that he saw Flock and not the technology itself as the problem. He credited license plate readers and traditional surveillance cameras with helping to identify people who committed crimes.
“Why do I want cameras? Because they work,” he said.
An earlier effort to replace ShotSpotter’s gunshot detection service with a Flock product without competitive bidding stalled. Polensek later criticized the administration for going around council to renew Cleveland’s ShotSpotter contract through the Board of Control.
“I hope they’re doing it right this time,” he said in an interview. “We said go out, let’s see what other vendors are available, what other systems [are] out there…We have to make sure it integrates with all the existing systems that we have in place already.”
Cleveland indicated in the request for proposals that it is flexible in how it awards the contract for license plate readers, gunshot detection and drones. Applicants can bid on just one or two of those services. Or they can bid to provide them all.
The license plate readers must be able to detect such features as car makes and models, license plates, bumper stickers and roof racks, according to the request. The gunshot detection must be able to map suspected shots.
The drones, which could be dispatched to the scene of 911 calls, must upload flight logs to a public portal. All the technology should be able to connect into the city’s Fusus software.
Flock is a big player in Northeast Ohio, court records show
Flock has been a major supplier of license plate readers in the Cleveland area. There are as many as 1,636 Flock cameras in Cuyahoga County, according to a 2025 ruling by a federal judge in a case that unearthed a trove of local records. Most police departments in the county have a contract with Flock, the judge wrote.
The Cuyahoga County Sheriff’s Department set up another network using the ELSAG license plate reader system sold by Leonardo, according to the order. The network is hosted by Chagrin Valley Dispatch.
Cleveland selected Flock as its license plate reader provider in 2023 after receiving bids from several companies, including Axon and Insight LPR, IT Commissioner Larry Jones II told City Council last month.
Other jurisdictions have parted ways with Flock and signed up with the competition. In Florida, the Pasco County sheriff is replacing Flock readers with technology offered by Axon, according to Tampa Bay 28. So has Benton County, Washington, the Tri-City Herald reported.
Cleveland’s safety director warned council in July that the six-month extension wouldn’t give the city enough time to vet a new vendor. The deadline to submit proposals is Sept. 8, and City Hall’s process for drafting contracts notoriously can be slow.
“They have to do it quick, because we only gave them a six-month extension for the license plate readers,” Polsensek told Signal Cleveland, “and I’m not going to extend that.”

sources.news_title: Flock Camera Vandalism Hits 23 States in August 2026
sources.text:
A wave of Flock Safety camera vandalism has now reached 23 states, according to a TechTimes report published August 10, 2026. People are cutting down, spray-painting, and disabling the automated license plate reader cameras in growing numbers. Law enforcement agencies have responded by using fusion centers to monitor the people doing the monitoring, raising serious civil liberties questions that go well beyond the vandalism itself.
What Is a Flock Safety Camera and How Does It Work?
Flock Safety cameras are automated license plate reader (ALPR) devices mounted on poles along roads, in neighborhoods, and near public buildings. They photograph every passing vehicle, capture the license plate number, and log the vehicle’s make, color, and timestamp. That data is uploaded to a cloud database accessible to law enforcement agencies.
The cameras don’t just read plates. They also record what Flock calls “vehicle fingerprint” data, details like roof racks, bumper stickers, and trailer hitches, to help officers identify vehicles even when plates are obscured. Thousands of police departments and homeowners associations across the country use the system. The company, founded in Atlanta in 2017, has grown rapidly by marketing itself as a force multiplier for understaffed departments.
How the data flows:
- A vehicle passes the camera
- The ALPR captures plate number and vehicle details in milliseconds
- Data uploads automatically to Flock’s cloud platform
- Officers search the database in real time or review footage after an incident
- Alerts can be triggered when a plate matches a “hot list” of flagged vehicles
The system is always on. It doesn’t wait for a crime to happen. Every car that passes gets logged.
Why Are Flock Safety Cameras Being Vandalized?
The vandalism isn’t random. It reflects deep, growing public distrust of pervasive surveillance technology operating with limited transparency or community input.
Critics argue Flock cameras create a de facto tracking system for everyday Americans who have done nothing wrong. Civil liberties groups point out that most communities never voted on whether to install them. Many residents only learn the cameras exist after they’re already up and running.
Common motivations cited by privacy advocates and researchers:
- Lack of consent: Cameras are often installed through police contracts or HOA decisions without broader public debate.
- Data retention fears: Flock retains location data for up to 30 days by default, but law enforcement agencies can access and share it more broadly through fusion centers.
- Racial equity concerns: Studies of ALPR technology have found disproportionate deployment in communities of color, raising questions about discriminatory surveillance.
- Mission creep: Systems sold as tools to solve car thefts have been used to track protesters, immigrants, and people attending political events.
The vandalism, then, is a form of protest. Whether you agree with the method or not, the underlying grievances are real and documented.
Flock Safety Camera Vandalism in August 2026: What the New Report Reveals
Flock Safety camera vandalism spreads to 23 states in August 2026, according to a TechTimes investigation published August 10, 2026. The report documents a coordinated surge in incidents, cameras cut from poles, lenses spray-painted, housings smashed, across states from the South to the Pacific Northwest.
This isn’t a handful of isolated incidents. Twenty-three states represent a geographic spread that suggests an organized or at least ideologically connected movement. The TechTimes report notes that online communities have circulated guides on identifying camera locations and disabling them without triggering immediate alerts.
“The scale of the vandalism signals something beyond individual frustration. It reflects a broader reckoning with how surveillance technology gets deployed in American communities.”, TechTimes, August 10, 2026
The vandalism is illegal and can result in criminal charges ranging from misdemeanor property damage to felony destruction of government equipment, depending on the jurisdiction.
Which States Are Affected by Flock Camera Vandalism?
As of the August 2026 TechTimes report, incidents have been confirmed in 23 states. The report does not name every state individually, but notes that the vandalism is concentrated in states with high Flock Safety deployment density, including states in the South, Midwest, and West Coast where the company has major law enforcement contracts.
States with the largest Flock Safety footprints, including Georgia, Texas, Florida, California, and Ohio, are among those where incidents have been reported. The spread into smaller states suggests the movement is growing beyond major metro areas into suburban and rural communities.
The Fusion Center Controversy: Surveilling the Surveillers
Here’s where the story gets significantly more complicated. Law enforcement agencies aren’t just repairing damaged cameras. According to the TechTimes report, fusion centers, the government’s network of intelligence-sharing hubs established after 9/11, are now being used to monitor and track individuals suspected of interfering with Flock cameras.
Fusion centers were created to share terrorism-related intelligence between federal, state, and local agencies. Using them to track camera vandals, or even people who are simply documenting camera locations, is a significant expansion of their original mandate.
Why this matters:
- Fusion centers operate with limited public oversight and minimal transparency requirements.
- Their involvement elevates what might be a local property crime into a matter of federal intelligence interest.
- Civil liberties organizations warn that the surveillance net may be catching legal activists, journalists, and researchers who are simply observing or photographing cameras in public spaces.
The ACLU and other groups have long raised concerns about fusion center overreach. Using them to monitor people who are themselves monitoring surveillance cameras creates a recursive loop that should concern anyone who values civil liberties, regardless of political affiliation.
How Much Does a Flock Safety Camera Cost?
Flock Safety operates on a subscription model rather than a one-time purchase. Municipalities and law enforcement agencies typically pay between $2,500 and $3,500 per camera per year, which includes hardware, installation, cloud storage, and software access.
For a small city deploying 50 cameras, that’s a potential annual cost of $125,000 to $175,000. Larger departments with hundreds of cameras can spend well into the millions annually. The subscription model means agencies are locked into ongoing payments, and canceling means losing access to historical data.
Private communities and HOAs can also purchase Flock cameras, often at similar price points, with data shared directly with local police departments.
Is Flock Safety Camera Worth It After the Vandalism Incidents?
For law enforcement agencies, the calculus is complicated. Flock cameras have a documented record of helping solve vehicle-related crimes. But the vandalism wave raises real operational and financial questions.
Choose Flock Safety if:
- Your department has a high volume of vehicle theft or hit-and-run cases
- You have the budget for ongoing subscription costs and replacement hardware
- Your community has had a transparent public conversation about deployment
Reconsider if:
- Your community has not had a public debate about surveillance policy
- You lack clear data retention and access policies
- You’re in an area where deployment may have disparate racial impact
The vandalism incidents themselves represent a financial liability. Replacing damaged cameras costs money. Deploying fusion center resources to investigate vandals costs more. At some point, communities need to ask whether the surveillance infrastructure is worth the social friction it’s generating.
Flock Safety Camera Alternatives
Flock Safety is the dominant player, but it’s not the only option. Several alternatives exist for communities that want ALPR capability with different privacy trade-offs.
- Motorola Solutions (Vigilant): A major competitor with a large law enforcement client base and similar ALPR functionality.
- Genetec AutoVu: An enterprise-grade ALPR system often used by larger municipalities with existing Genetec security infrastructure.
- Rekor Systems: Offers AI-enhanced vehicle recognition with some different data governance options.
- Local camera networks without ALPR: Some communities opt for standard surveillance cameras without automated plate reading, reducing the scope of data collection.
None of these alternatives fully resolve the underlying privacy concerns. The issue isn’t just which company makes the camera, it’s what policies govern the data once it’s collected.
How to Protect Flock Safety Cameras from Vandalism
Preventing vandalism requires both physical hardening and community trust-building. Physical fixes alone won’t solve a problem rooted in public distrust.
Physical protection measures:
- Install cameras at heights that require specialized equipment to reach
- Use tamper-resistant mounting hardware
